notes:
Natural Resources
- Definition: Physical supplies that exist in nature, including soil, water, air, plants, animals, and energy (actual and potential resources supplied by nature).
- Examples in Ethiopia: gold, platinum, potash, limestone, natural gas, coal, lakes, volcanic landscapes, waterfalls, timber, crop plants, coffee plantations, many species of animals and plants, and varied birdlife.

Renewable vs Non-renewable Resources
- Renewable: mainly living things and their products, plus sources such as sun, wind, water, geothermal heat, and biomass. These can be used, reused, and replaced when managed carefully. Examples: crop plants, trees, cattle, chickens.
- Non-renewable: natural substances not replaced at the same speed at which they are used up; they are finite resources. Examples: metals (gold, iron) and fossil fuels (oil, natural gas, coal).

Conservation
- Definition: the careful maintenance and wise use of natural resources to prevent them from disappearing; the act of preserving, guarding, or protecting the natural environment.
- Purpose: ensure non-renewable resources are used sparingly and renewable resources are appropriately managed so they last for an extended period into the future.

Conservation Biology
- A mission-oriented science that focuses on how to protect and restore biodiversity (the diversity of life on Earth).
- Biologists conserve species and save them from extinction through preservation of animals and plants in zoos and seed banks, and by stopping the destruction of natural habitats so populations can thrive.

Sustainable Management
- Conserving Ethiopia's non-renewable natural resources is economically advantageous, but mining metals and fossil fuels has a negative impact on the earth (e.g., contributing to climate change); using renewable energy sources is more beneficial to the planet.
- Even renewable resources can be lost if not managed carefully.
- Example sustainable practice: coppicing and maintaining a continual cycle of planting trees to replace the ones being cut down, bearing in mind the lag time for trees to grow.

The Importance of Conservation
- Protection of both renewable and non-renewable resources is critical for the survival of people.
- The knowledge and application of conservation is essential to sustainable management of natural resources.
summary: This section introduces natural resources and the application of biology to their conservation. Natural resources are the physical supplies that exist in nature - soil, water, air, plants, animals, and energy - and they are classified as renewable (mainly living things and natural sources such as sun, wind, water, geothermal heat, and biomass, which can be replaced when managed carefully) or non-renewable (finite substances such as metals like gold and iron, and fossil fuels like oil, natural gas, and coal, which are used up faster than they are replaced). Conservation is the careful maintenance and wise use of natural resources to prevent them from disappearing; it protects the environment so non-renewables are used sparingly and renewables are managed well so they last into the future. Conservation biology is a mission-oriented science focused on protecting and restoring biodiversity. Ethiopia holds rich natural resources (gold, platinum, potash, limestone, natural gas, coal, lakes, volcanic landscapes, waterfalls, timber, coffee, diverse crops, animals, and birds) whose economic exploitation must be balanced with environmental protection. Sustainable practice examples include coppicing and continual replanting of trees (bearing in mind the lag time for trees to grow), and biologists conserve species through zoos, seed banks, and preserving natural habitats to prevent extinction.

notes:
Food Security
- Definition (UN Committee on World Food Security): a state in which all people have physical, social, and economic access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food that meets their food preferences and dietary needs for an active and healthy life at all times.

Nutrition Security
- A situation whereby individuals have access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious foods, safe water, and adequate sanitation, the ability to access health care services, and knowledge of sound household and community practices in child care, food storage and preparation, and hygiene.

Requirements for Food Security
- Enough food is available for all in a country.
- All individuals have the capacity to buy food of acceptable quality.
- There is no barrier to access to food.

Food Insecurity
- Often rooted in poverty; has long-term impacts on the potential of families, communities, and countries to develop and prosper.
- Prolonged undernourishment slows growth, stunts cognitive development, and increases susceptibility to illness.

Types of Malnutrition
- Over-nutrition: too fat for height and age.
- Wasting: too thin for height.
- Stunting: too short for age.
- Micronutrient deficiencies may also occur even with otherwise good nutrition.

Role of Biology in Food Security
- Producing high-nutrient staple crops.
- Developing new products that can combat malnutrition.
- Improving food utilization.
- Biotechnologists design manufacturing processes and machinery used to produce food and drink, enabling products with consistent flavor, color, and texture to be produced in large quantities.

School-based Gardening as a Strategy
- Growing different vegetables in the school compound on the ground or in pots demonstrates how one can secure food in a small area and is a practical strategy for addressing food security.
summary: This section explains food and nutrition security and the role of biology in achieving them. Food security, as defined by the United Nations' Committee on World Food Security, is a state in which all people have physical, social, and economic access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food that meets their food preferences and dietary needs for an active and healthy life at all times. Food insecurity is rooted in poverty and has long-term impacts on the potential of families, communities, and countries to develop and prosper; prolonged undernourishment slows growth, stunts cognitive development, and increases susceptibility to illness. Nutrition security additionally requires safe water, adequate sanitation, access to health care, and knowledge of sound household and community practices in child care, food storage and preparation, and hygiene. Food security is ensured only when enough food is available for all, all individuals have the capacity to buy food of acceptable quality, and there is no barrier to access. Biology plays a key role in food security through producing high-nutrient staple crops, developing new products that combat malnutrition, and improving food utilization; biotechnologists design the manufacturing processes and machinery used to produce food and drink, ensuring consistent flavor, color, and texture in large quantities. The section also introduces types of malnutrition - over-nutrition, wasting (too thin for height/age), and stunting (too short for age) versus good nutrition. Practical activity involves school-based gardening as one strategy of addressing food security.

notes:
Role of Biology in Creating Conscious Citizens
- Biology expands awareness of the social, global, and environmental conditions.
- It empowers conscious citizens to assume personal responsibility by engaging in and being committed to initiating positive impact.

Biology, Technology and Sustainable Development
- The interplay of biology and technology (biotechnology) has become vital to facilitating sustainable development initiatives.
- Conscious citizens will use biotechnology applications to improve life and living on the planet.

Innovations by Conscious Citizen Biologists
- Developing innovative and cost-effective bio-based technologies.
- These technologies consume fewer resources, incorporate recycling, reuse components, and reduce production of wastes.
- They use strategies for sustaining a greener earth and improving food production.

Sustainability
- Represented by three dimensions: economic, social, and environmental.
- Commonly depicted either as pillars, embedded circles, or a popular Venn diagram of three overlapping circles.

Sustainable Development Practice
- Protecting, managing, and monitoring the existing resources of the land.
- Analysing soil, water, and air for chemical pollution.
- Finding ways to clean up pollution.
- Putting ethical decision making into action, ultimately to improve life and living on the planet.

notes:
Definition and Basics
- Biotechnology: the application of technologies that involve the use of living organisms, or products from living organisms, for the development of products that benefit humans.
- GMO (genetically modified organism): an organism that has received genetic material via recombinant DNA technology.
- Transgene: a gene from one species introduced into another species; such an organism is called a transgenic organism.

(i) Food Processing and Production
- Increasing food productivity using microorganisms.
- Single-cell protein (SCP): produced from waste materials such as molasses from sugar refining, petroleum by-products, and agricultural wastes.
- Pruteen: animal feed produced by mass culture of the bacterium Methylophilus methylotrophus.
- Mycoprotein: product made from the fungus Fusarium venenatum, with a filamentous texture making it suitable for meat substitutes.
- Spirulina: spiral-shaped cyanobacterium, harvested from lakes and ponds, an alternative to green plants as a primary nutrient source.
- Vitamins: Vitamin C was the first vitamin produced via fermentation by bacteria; vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) via propionic bacteria fermentation; vitamin B2 (Riboflavin) yield enhanced 100-300 fold by microbes.

(a) Dairy Products
- Cultured buttermilk: adds Streptococcus cremoris to pasteurized skim milk.
- Sour cream and yogurt: yogurt adds Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus bulgaricus to milk.
- Acidophilus milk: made by adding Lactobacillus acidophilus to sterile milk (sterilization prevents uncontrolled fermentation).
- Bulgarian milk: made by L. bulgaricus, similar to buttermilk but more acidic.

(b) Fermented Meats
- Lactobacillus plantarum and Pediococcus cerevisiae add flavor by fermenting meats such as salami, summer sausage, and Lebanon bologna; heterolactic acid fermentation preserves meat and gives tangy flavor.
- Fungi such as Penicillium and Aspergillus help produce the distinctive flavor of country hams.

(c) Beer, Wine, and Spirits
- Beer and wine: made by fermenting sugary juices; spirits (whiskey, gin, rum) by fermenting and then distilling.
- Distillation separates alcohol and other volatile substances from solid and nonvolatile substances.
- Strains of Saccharomyces are the fermenters for all alcoholic beverages.
- To make beer: malt barley to concentrate starch-digesting enzymes, crush and mix with hot water to produce mash, separate wort, add hops for flavoring, boil, then ferment with Saccharomyces.
- Wine: most made from grape juice, treated with sulfur dioxide to kill wild yeasts; add sugar and Saccharomyces, ferment, siphon and clear, bottle and age.
- Spirits: made from malted barley (Scotch whiskey), rye (rye whiskey, gin), corn (bourbon), wine/fruit juice (brandy), potatoes (vodka), molasses (rum); after fermentation, distilling raises alcohol content to 40-50% (vs ~12% wine, ~6% beer).

(d) Bread Making
- Microorganisms do three functions: leavening the dough, imparting flavor and odor, and conditioning the dough (workability).
- Leavening: release of gas producing a porous, spongy product; most common agent is baker's yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
- Yeast respires aerobically in dough; chief products of maltose fermentation are carbon dioxide and water (not alcohol).
- Other gas-formers: coliform bacteria, Clostridium species, heterofermentative lactic acid bacteria, wild yeasts.
- Microbial enzymes break down flour proteins (gluten) giving dough elasticity; kneading incorporates air.
- Example flavors: rye bread from lactic acid bacteria (Lactobacillus plantarum, L. brevis, L. bulgaricus, Leuconostoc mesenteroides, Streptococcus thermophilus); sourdough tang from Lactobacillus sanfranciscensis.

Genetic Engineering
- Genetic engineering: the process of transferring DNA from one organism into another, resulting in a genetic modification and production of a transgenic organism.

(a) Animal Breeding and Transgenic Animals/Plants
- Animal breeding addresses the genetic value of livestock by selecting for superior traits (growth rate, egg/meat/milk/wool production).
- Transgenic technology applications: enhancing prolificacy and reproductive performance, increasing feed utilization and growth rate, improving carcass composition, improving milk production/composition, modifying hair or fiber, increasing disease resistance.
- Gene transfer is a relatively rapid way of altering the genome of domestic livestock.

(b) Tissue Culture
- Tissue culture: biological research method in which fragments of tissue from an animal or plant are transferred to an artificial environment where they can continue to survive and function.
- Produces plants quickly and in large quantity; used for palm trees, orchids, bananas, carrots.
- Produces disease-free, high-quality planting material; important biotechnology for developing countries.

Health and Well-being
- Human drugs (insulin for diabetics, growth hormone for pituitary dwarfism, tissue plasminogen activator for heart attack victims) and animal drugs (bovine/porcine somatotropin) produced by fermentation of transgenic bacteria carrying the appropriate human, cow, or pig gene.

(a) Antibiotics Manufacture
- Antibiotics: complex organic compounds synthesized by microorganisms (most come from soil bacteria or fungi).
- Penicillin: produced by the mould fungus Penicillium, discovered by Sir Alexander Fleming in 1928; different mutant forms produce different penicillins (ampicillin, methicillin, oxacillin are chemically altered to be more effective).
- Streptomycin: produced by the actinomycete (filamentous soil bacterium) Streptomyces.
- Antibiotics act by disrupting cell wall production (bursting bacteria), interfering with protein synthesis, etc.; bacteriostatic stop reproduction, bacteriocidal kill bacteria.
- Antibiotics do not damage human cells (no cell walls, different protein structures) but may cause side effects such as allergic reactions.
- Some vaccines adaptable to mass production via fermentation: Bordetella pertussis, Salmonella typhi, Vibrio cholerae, Mycobacterium tuberculosis; toxoids for DT vaccines from Corynebacterium diphtheriae and Clostridium tetani.
- Fermenters: containers with steam/cold water to control temperature while culture is aerated.

(b) Biosensors
- Biosensors: in bioelectronics, living microorganisms (or their enzymes/organelles) linked with electrodes; biological reactions are converted into electrical currents.
- Applications: measure specific components in beer, monitor pollutants, detect flavor compounds, measure glucose, acetic acid, glutamic acid, ethanol, biochemical oxygen demand, cephalosporin, nicotinic acid, B vitamins.
- New immunochemical-based biosensors detect pathogens, herbicides, toxins, proteins, and DNA; many use streptavidin-biotin recognition.
- Example: handheld aflatoxin detection system for monitoring food quality (0.1-50 ppb in <2 min).

(c) Forensic Science
- Forensic biologists inspect crime scenes for evidence (blood, saliva, hair), analyze specimens focusing on DNA analysis, and use fingerprints.
- PCR (polymerase chain reaction) is a key forensic tool, plus gel electrophoresis for analyzing variable number tandem repeats (VNTR) loci; odds that two random individuals share the genetic pattern ~1 in 10 billion.
- Used to investigate crimes, paternity tests, and present findings in court.
- Bioinformatics makes evidence gathering easier and more reliable with computational tools.

Biomining (Microbiological Mining)
- Biohydrometallurgy: the use of microbes to extract metals from ores (as mineral-rich ores decrease, methods extract from less concentrated sources).
- Thiobacillus ferrooxidans: chemolithotrophic acidophilic bacterium that oxidizes sulfur binding copper, zinc, lead, uranium into sulfide minerals, releasing the pure metal; oxidizes iron sulfide to release iron.
- Combinations of T. ferrooxidans with T. thiooxidans degrade some copper and iron ores more rapidly; Leptospirillum ferrooxidans and T. organoparus together degrade pyrite (FeS2) and chalcopyrite (CuFeS2).

Environmental Applications
(a) Solid Waste Treatment: Composting and Landfill
- Landfill: refuse deposited in large holes; non-biodegradable components (metals, plastics, rubble) remain indefinitely, while biodegradable material (food waste, textiles, paper) decomposes over time (can take decades).
- Aerobic processes give way to anaerobic ones, generating methane; modern landfills remove methane (avoids fire/explosion hazard, can be used as fuel).
- Composting: fungi and bacteria, especially actinomycetes, break down organic matter to CO2, water, and humus.

(b) Wastewater Treatment
- Aim: removal of undesirable substances and hazardous microorganisms so water may safely enter a watercourse; reduces incidence of waterborne diseases such as cholera.
- Sewage: liquid wastes that contain faecal matter (human or animal).
- Effectiveness judged by reduction of biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), a measure of oxygen needed by microorganisms to oxidize organic content; high BOD indicates pollution.
- Primary treatment: physical - removal of floating objects followed by sedimentation (removes up to one-third of BOD).
- Secondary treatment: microbial oxidation reducing BOD 80-85% (trickling filter over stones/plastic with biofilm of bacteria, protozoans, fungi, algae) or activated sludge process (aerated tanks seeded with mixed microbial sludge; Zoogloea secretes slime forming flocs); treated water chlorinated to remove pathogens.
- Surplus sludge undergoes anaerobic digestion producing methane and CO2; dewatered and used as soil conditioner (care that sludge has no toxic heavy metals).

(c) Bioremediation
- Bioremediation: the use of living organisms or their products for detoxification and degradation of environmental pollutants; also called biodegradation.
- Genetically engineered bacteria break down toxic pollutants into harmless compounds; e.g., mercury-resistant bacteria process metallic mercury (damages the nervous system) into a nontoxic compound.
- Biotransformation: enzymes from a microorganism modify a toxic pollutant by altering/transforming its structure; may result in biodegradation or oxidation/reduction rendering heavy metals less toxic.

(d) Biofuels
- Biofuel (chiefly ethanol) obtained by fermentation of plant material; corn is currently the substrate of choice, crop residues could boost yields.
- Crop residues (cellulose/hemicellulose from plant material left after harvest) are polymers of glucose, xylose, mannose, galactose, arabinose; engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments xylose and engineered E. coli expressing Zymomonas mobilis genes ferments all five sugars.
- Research aims to replace harsh thermochemical treatment with fungal cellulases/hemicellulases and enzymes from thermoacidophiles.

(e) Biogas Production
- Biogas: combustible gas (mostly methane with some carbon dioxide) produced by bacteria and archaeans from organic matter in fermenters.
- Three communities of anaerobic microbes: first converts raw organic waste into organic acids, alcohol, hydrogen, CO2 (Eubacteria); second uses acids/alcohol to produce acetate, CO2, hydrogen (Eubacteria); third are Archaea called methanogens producing methane.
- Methanogen reactions: CO2 + 4H2 -> CH4 + 2H2O (reduction of CO2) or CH3COOH -> CH4 + CO2 (splitting ethanoic acid).
- Advantages: biogas is a fuel to cook food and light lamps; slurry forms a soil conditioner (manure); much cheaper than LPG for home use.

(f) Composting
- Composting: an aerobic, microbe-driven process converting solid organic wastes into a stable, sanitary, humus-like material reduced in bulk.
- Carried out in a packed bed of solid organic particles; free access to air essential; arranged in static piles, aerated piles, covered tunnels, or rotating bioreactors (drums).
- Basic reaction: oxidation of mixed organic substrates with oxygen to produce CO2, water, and other organic by-products.

Industrial Applications
(a) Enzymes
- Produced by commercial fermentation using feed stocks such as corn-steep liquor or molasses; common organisms: fungi (Aspergillus) or bacteria (Bacillus), chosen because they are non-pathogenic and do not produce antibiotics.
- Extracellular enzymes: filtered from feedstock and extracted; intracellular enzymes: organisms crushed and enzymes extracted with water or solvents.

(b) Biological Washing Powders
- Proteases (protein-digesting) and lipases (fat-digesting) enzymes remove protein and fat stains (blood, egg, gravy, grease) by digesting large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones that pass out of the cloth.
- Save energy: wash at lower temperatures; but enzymes denature in hotter water, losing effectiveness.

Agricultural Applications
(a) Biopesticides
- Biological agents (bacteria, fungi, viruses, or their components) used to kill susceptible insects.
- Bacteria: Bacillus thuringiensis (wide variety of crops, fruits, shade trees, ornamentals) and Bacillus popilliae (Japanese beetle larvae); Pseudomonas fluorescens (with B. thuringiensis toxin gene) on maize to suppress black cutworms.
- Viruses: nuclear polyhedrosis virus (NPV), granulosis virus (GV), cytoplasmic polyhedrosis virus (CPV) - occluded viruses protected in the environment.
- Fungi: Beauveria bassiana (Colorado potato beetle), Metarhizium anisopliae (froghopper in sugarcane), Verticillium lecanii and Entomophthora (aphids in greenhouse and field).

(b) Ti Plasmid as a Vector
- Agrobacterium tumefaciens has the Ti plasmid, causing tumours in plants it infects; the glyphosate resistance gene is inserted into the Ti plasmid along with an antibiotic resistance gene, re-inserted into A. tumefaciens; plant cells exposed and cultured on antibiotic plates, only cells that took up the plasmid grow.

(c) Insect-resistant Crops
- Genetically modified plants protected against insect pests: maize against corn borer, cotton against boll weevil, tobacco against tobacco bud worm (not yet commercial).
- Possible detrimental effects: evolution of resistance by pests, effects on other insects, transfer of added gene to other plant species; however less pesticide is used and only insects that actually eat the crop are affected.

(d) Pest-resistant Crops
- Bt-cotton: genes of Bacillus thuringiensis inserted into cotton to develop protein very toxic to insects; leads to less pest attack and significantly more production.

(e) Transgenic Animals
- Some proteins require a eukaryotic animal host for proper processing; genes cloned and expressed in sheep, goats, chickens, mice.
- Human proteins expressed in milk of transgenic sheep and goats; some in chicken eggs; mice used extensively for expressing recombinant genes and studying mutations.

(f) Transgenic Plants
- Manipulating plant DNA (creating GMOs) creates desirable traits: disease resistance, herbicide/pesticide resistance, better nutritional value, better shelf life.
- Staples like corn, potatoes, and tomatoes were the first crop plants genetically engineered.
- Transgenic plants closely monitored by government agencies for human consumption and ecological safety.

(g) Herbicide Resistance
- Glyphosate kills any green plant but becomes harmless in soil; a gene for an enzyme that breaks down glyphosate can be introduced into plant cell culture, leading to reduced herbicide use.

Cloning
- Cloning: method of producing identical copies of genes, cells, or organisms; a clone is a group of genetically identical organisms or cells produced by asexual reproduction or artificially.
- Advantage: can make large numbers of plants or animals, exact copies of a parent with desirable characteristics; sometimes used to produce skin or other tissues for treatment.
- Animal cloning: dividing early embryos into several pieces; hard to predict which produce desirable characteristics.
- Dolly the sheep: first successful reproductive cloning of an adult with known characteristics - udder cells from a donor sheep fused with enucleated egg cells using electricity, developed like a zygote, implanted into a surrogate mother; Dolly is genetically identical to the donor sheep.

Biological Warfare
- Biological warfare (BW), also known as germ warfare: the use of biological toxins or infectious agents (bacteria, viruses, fungi) to kill or incapacitate humans, animals, or plants as an act of war.
- Biological weapons: any microorganism or toxin (poisonous compounds produced by microorganisms) found in nature; bioterrorism ranges from hoaxes to actual use; environment contamination can create a long-term threat.
summary: This section surveys the wide-ranging applications of biotechnology - the use of living organisms or their products to develop products that benefit humans. Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) have received genetic material via recombinant DNA technology; a gene moved from one species into another is a transgene, making the recipient a transgenic organism. Applications include: (1) Food processing and production, increasing food productivity using microorganisms such as Methylophilus methylotrophus for Pruteen, the cyanobacterium Spirulina as a protein source, the fungus Fusarium venenatum for mycoprotein (meat substitutes), vitamin production via fermentation (Vitamin C first, then B12 and B2 by microbes), and the making of dairy products (buttermilk, sour cream, yogurt), fermented meats, beer, wine, spirits, and bread using strains of Saccharomyces and lactic acid bacteria. (2) Genetic engineering, including animal breeding with superior traits, transgenic farm animals, and plant/animal tissue culture for large-scale, disease-free propagation. (3) Health and well-being, producing human and animal drugs (insulin, growth hormones) via fermentation of transgenic bacteria, manufacturing antibiotics (penicillin from Penicillium, streptomycin from Streptomyces), developing biosensors that convert biological reactions into electrical signals for detecting pathogens, toxins, glucose and other metabolites, and using forensic science with DNA analysis, PCR, fingerprints and gel electrophoresis for crime investigation and paternity testing. (4) Biomining (biohydrometallurgy) using microbes such as Thiobacillus ferrooxidans to leach and extract metals (copper, zinc, lead, uranium, iron) from low-grade ores. (5) Environmental applications: composting and landfill management with methanogenesis, wastewater treatment (primary physical treatment reducing BOD, secondary biological treatment by trickling filters or activated sludge with Zoogloea), bioremediation/biodegradation and biotransformation to clean pollutants, biofuel (ethanol) production by fermentation of plant material, and biogas (methane) production by three microbial communities including methanogens. (6) Industrial applications: production of enzymes (proteases, lipases, pectinases, amylases) used in washing powders, food and textiles. (7) Agricultural applications: biopesticides (Bacillus thuringiensis, fungal and viral agents), use of Agrobacterium tumefaciens Ti plasmid to introduce genes such as glyphosate resistance into crops, insect-resistant crops, pest-resistant crops (Bt-cotton), transgenic plants and animals expressing recombinant proteins, herbicide resistance, cloning (including Dolly the sheep), and biological warfare/germ warfare as an unethical and prohibited use of biological toxins and infectious agents.

--- -The Future of Applied Biology: Genomics and Personalized Medicine ---
  • Genomics is the study of the structure, function, evolution, and mapping of an organism's entire set of DNA (genome).
  • Proteomics is the large-scale study of proteins, their functions, and how they interact.
  • Personalized Medicine uses an individual's genomic data to predict their susceptibility to disease and how they will respond to specific drugs.
  • Pharmacogenomics is a key application that combines pharmacology and genomics to develop safe and effective drug doses and selection based on a person's genetic makeup.
  • This approach is moving medicine away from a "one-size-fits-all" model to a highly targeted, patient-centric model.
summary: This emerging field focuses on using a patient’s complete genetic and protein information (genomics and proteomics) to tailor medical treatments, dosages, and preventative measures for maximum efficacy and minimal side effects.
keywords:
• Genomics: The study of an organism's entire genome.
  • Proteomics: The large-scale study of proteins.
  • Personalized Medicine: Medical model tailored to an individual’s unique genetic profile.
  • Pharmacogenomics: The study of how genes affect a person's response to drugs.
solved_examples: Question: Explain the core idea behind the use of pharmacogenomics in medicine. Solution: The core idea is that an individual's genes affect how their body metabolizes or responds to a drug. Pharmacogenomics analyzes these genes to predict the best drug and dosage for a patient, thereby maximizing treatment effectiveness while reducing the risk of adverse side effects.

notes:
What are Eubacteria?
- Eubacteria literally means 'true bacteria'. They are prokaryotic, unicellular organisms with no nuclear membrane, mitochondria, Golgi bodies, or endoplasmic reticulum, and they reproduce by asexual division.

General Characteristics
- Omnipresent: found in soil, air, and water.
- Unicellular, prokaryotic microorganisms.
- Cell bears a thick rigid cell wall (peptidoglycan) outside the plasma membrane.
- Great variation in mode of nutrition: autotrophic or heterotrophic (parasitic, saprophytic, or symbiotic).
- Lack a true nucleus (no nuclear membrane and nucleolus).
- Lack mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, plastids, and endoplasmic reticulum.
- Lack true chlorophyll, but a few photosynthetic bacteria have a special pigment called bacteriochlorophyll.
- Both DNA and RNA are present in the bacterial cell.

Eukaryotes vs Prokaryotes
- Prokaryotes: unicellular organisms lacking a membrane-enclosed nucleus.
- Eukaryotes: organisms whose cells have a nucleus enclosed within a nuclear envelope, with complex membranous organelles in the cytoplasmic matrix; a cytoskeleton made of microtubules, microfilaments, and intermediate filaments gives shape and is involved in movement, intracellular transport, and reproduction (mitosis and meiosis).

Structure of a Bacterial Cell (prokaryote)
- Appendages: flagella, fimbriae.
- Glycocalyx: capsule or slime layer.
- Cell envelope: cell wall and cell membrane.
- Cytoplasmic matrix: ribosomes, inclusions, nucleoid/chromosome, actin cytoskeleton.
- Endospore (in some).

Classification by Shape
- Cocci (sing. coccus): spherical bacteria.
- Bacilli (sing. bacillus): rod-shaped bacteria.
- Spirochaetes: spiral or corkscrew-shaped bacteria (e.g., comma-shaped Vibrio cholerae).
- Arrangement patterns (pairs, clusters, chains) are also used (e.g., Streptococcus = chains, Staphylococcus = clusters).

Classification by Cell Wall - Gram's Stain
- Gram's staining: a differential staining test for distinguishing bacteria, developed by Hans Christian Gram in 1884. Steps: (1) heat fix bacteria to slide, (2) apply primary stain (crystal violet), (3) add mordant (Gram's iodine), (4) rapid decolorization with ethanol/acetone, (5) counterstain with safranin.
- Gram-positive: retain crystal violet (purple) because of the thick peptidoglycan layer (20-80 nm) containing teichoic and lipoteichoic acids; no outer membrane; more penetrable to molecules. Examples: all staphylococci, all streptococci, some listeria.
- Gram-negative: lose crystal violet and take the red counterstain; thin peptidoglycan layer (8-11 nm), outer membrane, lipopolysaccharide, lipoprotein, porin proteins, extensive periplasmic space; less penetrable. Examples: most enteric bacteria.
- Key cell-wall terms: peptidoglycan (rigid sheet of N-acetylglucosamine, N-acetylmuramic acid, and amino acids) and endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide portion of the cell envelope of gram-negative bacteria, toxic to humans when solubilized).

Nutritional Types of Bacteria
- Phototrophs: use light energy; Chemotrophs: obtain energy from oxidizing chemical compounds.
- Lithotrophs ('rock-eaters'): use reduced inorganic substances as electron source; Organotrophs: extract electrons from reduced organic compounds.
- Five nutritional classes:
  1. Photolithoautotrophs (photoautotrophs): CO2 carbon source, light energy, inorganic electron donor (e.g., cyanobacteria, purple and green sulfur bacteria).
  2. Photoorganoheterotrophs: organic carbon, light, organic electron donor (e.g., purple nonsulfur bacteria).
  3. Chemolithoautotrophs: CO2, inorganic chemicals, inorganic electron donor (sulfur-, hydrogen-, iron-oxidizing bacteria, methanogens, nitrifying bacteria).
  4. Chemolithoheterotrophs: organic carbon, inorganic chemicals, inorganic electron donor (some sulfur-oxidizing bacteria like Beggiatoa).
  5. Chemoorganoheterotrophs (chemoheterotrophs): organic carbon, organic chemicals, organic electron donor (most nonphotosynthetic microbes, most pathogens, fungi, many protists and archaea).

Reproduction in Bacteria
- Binary fission (asexual): cell doubles in mass, chromosome replicates, the two DNA molecules separate, a partition (septum) forms at midcell, separating the mother cell into two genetically identical daughter cells. Bacteria lack a mitotic spindle.
- Conjugation (asexual gene transfer): two cells of different mating types come together and genetic material transfers (unlike transformation and transduction, conjugation involves contact). In E. coli: donor F+ cells carry the F (fertility) factor (about 20 genes, can be a plasmid or part of the chromosome); F+ cell produces a sex pilus that binds to an F- cell forming a conjugation bridge; F plasmid replicates and a single strand transfers from donor to recipient; F- cell is converted to F+. F plasmids may carry antibiotic resistance genes.

Common Bacterial Diseases (agent / transmission)
- Pertussis: Bordetella pertussis, Gram-negative rod, upper respiratory tract, airborne.
- Meningococcal meningitis: Neisseria meningitidis, Gram-negative diplococcus, upper respiratory tract and meninges, airborne.
- Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, acid-fast, lungs, bones, other organs, airborne.
- Typhoid fever: Salmonella typhi, Gram-negative rod, intestine, blood, gall bladder, food and water.
- Cholera: Vibrio cholerae, Gram-negative rod (comma-shaped), intestine, food and water.
- Tetanus: Clostridium tetani, Gram-positive spore-forming anaerobic rod, nerves at synapse, soil.
- Syphilis: Treponema pallidum, spirochete, skin and cardiovascular organs, sexual contact.
- Gonorrhoea: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Gram-negative diplococcus, urethra, cervix, fallopian tubes, epididymis, eyes, pharynx, sexual contact.
- Leprosy: Mycobacterium leprae, acid-fast, skin, bones, peripheral nerves, contact.
summary: This section describes Eubacteria ('true bacteria'), the prokaryotic, unicellular microorganisms that lack a nuclear membrane, mitochondria, Golgi bodies, and endoplasmic reticulum and reproduce by asexual division. Their main characteristics include being omnipresent (in soil, air, and water), having a thick rigid peptidoglycan cell wall outside the plasma membrane, lacking a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, containing both DNA and RNA, and showing great variation in nutrition (autotrophic or heterotrophic - parasitic, saprophytic, or symbiotic). Photosynthetic bacteria possess a special chlorophyll called bacteriochlorophyll. The cellular structure includes external structures (glycocalyx/capsule/slime layer, flagella, fimbriae/pili) and internal structures (cytoplasmic matrix, ribosomes, inclusions, nucleoid/chromosome, endospore). Bacteria are classified by cell shape into cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod-shaped), and spirochaetes (spiral/corkscrew; comma-like Vibrio included). Using the Gram stain technique (developed by Hans Christian Gram in 1884) bacteria are grouped as Gram-positive (purple, thick peptidoglycan layer, e.g., all staphylococci, streptococci, some listeria) or Gram-negative (red counterstain, thin peptidoglycan layer plus lipopolysaccharide and outer membrane, less penetrable). Major nutritional types are photolithoautotrophs (cyanobacteria), chemolithoautotrophs (nitrifying, sulfur, iron bacteria, methanogens), and chemoorganoheterotrophs (most pathogens, fungi, many protists and archaea). Bacteria reproduce asexually mainly by binary fission, and some exchange genes by conjugation (transfer of F-plasmid DNA through a sex pilus from donor F+ to recipient F- cells). Common bacterial diseases include pertussis, meningococcal meningitis, tuberculosis, typhoid fever, cholera, tetanus, syphilis, gonorrhoea, and leprosy. Archaea are distinguished from bacteria by evolutionary history, genetics, metabolism, and cell wall/membrane composition.

notes:
Bacterial cells are very minute and therefore studied under the electron microscope.

External Structures
- Appendages: flagella (for motility) and fimbriae (hairlike attachment structures).
- Glycocalyx: capsule or slime layer outside the cell wall.

Cell Envelope
- Cell wall: rigid layer, containing peptidoglycan.
- Cell membrane: plasma membrane inside the wall.

Internal Structures (in the cytoplasmic matrix)
- Ribosomes (site of protein synthesis).
- Inclusions (stored materials).
- Nucleoid / chromosome (bacterial DNA).
- Actin cytoskeleton.
- Endospore (dormant, resistant structure in some bacteria).

Diagram Flowchart of the Prokaryotic Cell
- Appendages -> Fimbriae; Glycocalyx -> Capsule, slime layer; Cell envelope -> Cell wall, cell membrane; Cytoplasmic matrix -> Ribosomes, inclusions, nucleoid/chromosome, actin cytoskeleton; Endospore.

Eukaryotic Microbes (comparison)
- Have eukaryotic cells with complex membranous organelles in the cytoplasmic matrix and most genetic material within membrane-delimited nuclei.
- Each organelle has a distinctive structure related to specific functions.
- A cytoskeleton composed of microtubules, microfilaments, and intermediate filaments gives shape, and is involved in cell movement, intracellular transport, and reproduction.
- When eukaryotes reproduce, genetic material is distributed between cells by mitosis and meiosis.

Points for Comparison (eukaryotes vs prokaryotes)
- Presence/absence of nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
- Presence/absence of a cell wall and its composition.
- Method of reproduction (binary fission vs mitosis/meiosis).
summary: This section describes the structure of the bacterial cell as revealed by electron microscopy, since bacteria are too small to be studied with the light microscope. Some structures are external to the cell wall and others internal. The general structural plan of the prokaryotic cell includes appendages (flagella and fimbriae), a glycocalyx (capsule or slime layer), a cell envelope composed of the cell wall and cell membrane, and internal features in the cytoplasmic matrix such as ribosomes, inclusions, the nucleoid/chromosome, an actin cytoskeleton, and (in some) an endospore. The section also contrasts the eukaryotic cell, which has a nucleus containing most of its genetic material, a variety of complex membranous organelles, and a cytoskeleton of microtubules, microfilaments, and intermediate filaments used for shape, movement, intracellular transport, and reproduction (mitosis and meiosis).

notes:
Classification of bacteria based on morphology uses: cell shape, nature of multicellular aggregates, motility, formation of spores, and reaction to the Gram stain.

Three Main Bacterial Shapes
- Cocci (sing. coccus): spherical bacteria.
- Bacilli (sing. bacillus): rod-shaped bacteria.
- Spirochaetes: spiral or corkscrew-shaped bacteria.
- Comma-shaped cells: e.g., Vibrio cholerae.

Examples
- Streptococcus: chains of cocci.
- Lactobacillus: rods important in dairy products.
- Spiral-shaped bacteria cause diseases such as syphilis (Treponema pallidum).

Bacterial Cell Wall Anatomy (terms to describe)
- Outer membrane: membrane outside the thin peptidoglycan layer of gram-negative bacteria.
- Periplasmic space: space between the inner (plasma) membrane and the outer membrane.
- Envelope: the cell wall and cell membrane considered together.
- Teichoic acid: polymer found in the cell walls of gram-positive bacteria.
- Lipopolysaccharide (LPS): molecule in the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria (endotoxin portion).
- Porin protein: channel-forming protein in the outer membrane allowing passage of small molecules.
- Peptidoglycan: structural polymer of the bacterial cell wall.

Protoplasts vs Spheroplasts
- Protoplast: bacterial cell whose cell wall has been completely removed (works for gram-positive).
- Spheroplast: bacterial cell with a partially removed cell wall (gram-negative cells, which retain the outer membrane).

Role of the Cell Wall
- Protects the cell against lysis (osmotic rupture); demonstrated experimentally by removing the wall and observing cell bursting in hypotonic conditions.
summary: This section covers the classification of bacteria based on morphology. Morphological features used for classifying bacteria include cell shape, the nature of multicellular aggregates, motility, spore formation, and reaction to the Gram stain. Bacterial cells can be grouped into three main shapes: cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod-shaped), and spirochaetes (spiral or corkscrew-shaped), with comma-shaped cells such as Vibrio cholera also recognized. The cell wall is described, including distinctions between protoplasts and spheroplasts, and the roles of the outer membrane, periplasmic space, teichoic acid, lipopolysaccharide, and porin proteins.

notes:
Autotrophs
- Obtain their carbon from inorganic CO2.
- Photoautotrophs: obtain energy from sunlight.
- Chemoautotrophs: harvest energy from inorganic chemicals.

Heterotrophs
- Obtain at least some carbon from organic molecules such as glucose.
- Photoheterotrophs: obtain energy from sunlight.
- Chemoheterotrophs: harvest energy from organic molecules.

Electron Sources
- Lithotrophs ('rock-eaters'): reduced inorganic substances as electron source.
- Organotrophs: extract electrons from reduced organic compounds.

Energy Sources
- Light energy, or energy derived from oxidizing organic or inorganic molecules.

Five Nutritional Classes of Bacteria (carbon/energy/electron source)
1. Photolithoautotrophs (photoautotrophs): CO2 / light / inorganic electron donor. Examples: cyanobacteria, purple and green sulfur bacteria (which cannot oxidize water but extract electrons from hydrogen, hydrogen sulfide, elemental sulfur).
2. Photoorganoheterotrophs: organic carbon / light / organic electron donor. Examples: purple nonsulfur bacteria, green nonsulfur bacteria; common in polluted lakes and streams; some can grow as photolithoautotrophs with molecular hydrogen.
3. Chemolithoautotrophs: CO2 / inorganic chemicals / inorganic electron donor. Examples: sulfur-oxidizing bacteria, hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria, methanogens, nitrifying bacteria, iron-oxidizing bacteria.
4. Chemolithoheterotrophs: organic carbon / inorganic chemicals / inorganic electron donor. Example: some sulfur-oxidizing bacteria (Beggiatoa).
5. Chemoorganoheterotrophs (chemoheterotrophs or chemoorganotrophs): organic carbon / organic chemicals / organic electron donor. Nearly all pathogenic microorganisms; most nonphotosynthetic microbes, fungi, many protists and archaea.

Ecological Importance
- Chemolithotrophs contribute greatly to chemical transformations of elements (e.g., conversion of ammonia to nitrate, or sulfur to sulfate) that continually occur in ecosystems.
- Frequently the same organic nutrient satisfies carbon, energy, and electron requirements.
summary: Bacteria have evolved many mechanisms to acquire the energy and nutrients needed for growth. They are classified by their primary sources of carbon, energy, and electrons into five nutritional classes. Autotrophs obtain carbon from inorganic CO2 and include photoautotrophs (energy from sunlight) and chemoautotrophs (energy from inorganic chemicals). Heterotrophs obtain some carbon from organic molecules and include photoheterotrophs (sunlight) and chemoheterotrophs (organic molecules). Electron sources define lithotrophs (reduced inorganic substances) and organotrophs (reduced organic compounds). The five classes are: photolithoautotrophs (e.g., cyanobacteria, purple/green sulfur bacteria), photoorganoheterotrophs (purple/green nonsulfur bacteria), chemolithoautotrophs (sulfur-, hydrogen-, iron-oxidizing bacteria, methanogens, nitrifying bacteria), chemolithoheterotrophs (e.g., Beggiatoa), and chemoorganoheterotrophs (nearly all pathogenic microorganisms, most fungi, many protists and archaea). Nearly all pathogens are chemoorganoheterotrophs, while chemolithotrophs contribute greatly to elemental transformations such as the conversion of ammonia to nitrate or sulfur to sulfate.

notes:
Binary Fission (asexual reproduction)
- Most bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission after a period of growth in which the cell doubles in mass.
- The chromosome (DNA) replicates and the two DNA molecules separate.
- Unlike eukaryotic cells, bacteria lack a mitotic spindle to separate replicated chromosomes; segregation involves specialized chromosome-associated proteins.
- Cell fission at midcell involves synthesis of a partition (septum) that separates the mother cell into two genetically identical daughter cells.

Conjugation (asexual genetic exchange requiring contact)
- Two cells of different mating types come together and genetic material is transferred from one to the other.
- Contrast: transformation and transduction do not require cell contact; conjugation involves contact between two cells.
- Best studied in E. coli. Donor cells are F+ (have the F factor, 'F' for fertility; ~20 genes); recipient cells are F-.
- The F factor can exist as a plasmid or be part of the bacterial chromosome.
- Certain F genes encode sex pili - long, hairlike extensions projecting from the cell surface.
- The sex pilus recognizes and binds to an F- cell, forming a cytoplasmic conjugation bridge.
- The F plasmid replicates itself and DNA is transferred from donor to recipient through the bridge.
- F plasmids may carry other genes, including antibiotic resistance.
- After transfer, the F- cell is converted to F+.

Common Bacterial Diseases (disease / causative agent / transmission)
- Pertussis: Bordetella pertussis, airborne.
- Meningococcal meningitis: Neisseria meningitidis, airborne.
- Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, airborne.
- Typhoid fever: Salmonella typhi, food and water.
- Cholera: Vibrio cholerae, food and water.
- Tetanus: Clostridium tetani, soil.
- Syphilis: Treponema pallidum, sexual.
- Gonorrhoea: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, sexual.
- Leprosy: Mycobacterium leprae, contact.
summary: This section covers reproduction of bacteria, both asexual reproduction via binary fission and the specialized genetic exchange of conjugation. In binary fission, the cell doubles in mass, the chromosome replicates, the DNA molecules separate (without a mitotic spindle), and a partition (septum) synthesized at midcell separates the mother cell into two genetically identical daughter cells. Conjugation transfers genetic material through cell contact: in E. coli, donor F+ cells carry the F (fertility) factor (about 20 genes, as a plasmid or integrated into the chromosome); certain F genes encode sex pili, hairlike extensions that bind to an F- cell and form a cytoplasmic conjugation bridge; the F plasmid replicates and transfers a single DNA strand to the recipient, converting it to F+. Conjugation is distinguished from transformation and transduction by requiring direct cell contact. The section also lists common bacterial diseases with causes, organs affected, and mode of transmission.

notes:
This section describes a general method for isolating bacteria from environmental or food samples. The process involves:
1.  **Sample collection:** Collecting a sample (e.g., soil, food).
2.  **Serial dilution:** Diluting the sample to reduce the density of microorganisms.
3.  **Plating:** Plating the diluted samples on artificial media to separate individual bacterial cells.
4.  **Purification:** Isolating single colonies from the initial plates and transferring them to new media to obtain pure cultures.
5.  **Characterization:** Examining the purified isolates for morphological characteristics (shape, gram nature, arrangement, motility) and biochemical activities.
6.  **Identification:** Using molecular techniques (like DNA analysis) for further identification.
summary: This section outlines the standard technique for isolating microorganisms (bacteria or fungi) from a sample. The method involves serial dilution to separate organisms, plating on artificial media to obtain isolated colonies, purifying the cultures, and then characterizing them through morphological and biochemical tests, with final identification often confirmed by molecular techniques.
keywords: • Serial dilution: A technique for reducing the concentration of microorganisms in a sample by systematically diluting it, often used to obtain isolated colonies on a plate.

Renowned Microbiologists/Parasitologists in Ethiopia
- Ethiopian microbiologists and parasitologists have contributed research on communicable diseases, soil and plant microbiology, and food fermentation to the world of science.
- Students should search for, study the works of a renowned Ethiopian microbiologist/parasitologist, and evaluate the contribution of their research.

Unit Summary on Microorganisms
- Microorganisms are very diverse and found in all three domains of life: Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya.
- Archaea and bacteria are classified as prokaryotes because they lack a cellular nucleus.
- Archaea differ from bacteria in evolutionary history, genetics, metabolic pathways, and cell wall and membrane composition.
- Archaea inhabit nearly every environment on earth, but no archaea have been identified as human pathogens.

Eukaryotes studied in microbiology
- Algae: plant-like organisms, unicellular or multicellular, deriving energy via photosynthesis.
- Protozoa: unicellular organisms with complex cell structures; most are motile.
- Fungi: microscopic fungi are studied in mycology.
- Helminths: parasitic worms.

Technique: Microbial Isolation
- Microorganisms are isolated from environmental or food samples by weighing a sample (e.g., 10 g) and dissolving in distilled water (e.g., 90 ml) to make a serial dilution before plating on media.

notes:
Definition
- Archaea (archaeans): species in the Domain Archaea similar to bacteria - unicellular, microscopic organisms living as producers or decomposers.

General Characteristics of Archaea
- Prokaryotic.
- Single-celled organisms.
- Lack membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
- Lack true peptidoglycan in their cell walls.
- Cell membrane lipids have branched hydrocarbon chains.
- Many are found in extreme environments.

Major Groups of Archaea (based on physiology)
1. Methanogens: strictly anaerobic; generate methane by degrading organic molecules; isolated from waterlogged soils, lake sediments, marshes, marine sediments, and the gastrointestinal tracts of animals including humans; members of the anaerobic food chain.
2. Extreme halophiles: grow in highly saline environments (Great Salt Lake, Dead Sea, salt evaporation ponds, surfaces of salt-preserved foods); generally obligate aerobes.
3. Extreme thermophiles (hyperthermophiles): found near volcanic vents and fissures releasing sulfurous gases and hot vapors; optimum temperatures usually above 80 degrees C; can be obligate aerobes, facultative aerobes, or obligate anaerobes. Record temperature ~121 degrees C.
4. Thermophilic extreme acidophiles: e.g., Thermoplasma and Picrophilus, growing in extremely acidic, hot environments.

Classification Note
- These groupings are based on physiological characteristics, so they are not phylogenetic (evolutionary) classifications.
- The phylogenetic tree based on 16S ribosomal RNA genes reveals a split of Archaea into two phyla: Crenarchaeota and Euryarchaeota.

How Archaea Differ from Bacteria
- Identified as distinct prokaryotes on the basis of unique rRNA sequences.
- Lack true peptidoglycan in cell walls.
- Cell membrane lipids have branched hydrocarbon chains.
- The initial amino acid in their polypeptide chains, coded by the AUG start codon, is methionine (as in eukaryotes), in contrast to the N-formylmethionine used by bacteria.
- Multiply by binary fission, budding, fragmentation, or other mechanisms.
- Nutritionally aerobic, facultative anaerobic, or strictly anaerobic; chemolithoautotroph to organotroph.

Beneficial Aspects of Archaea
1. Source of enzymes added to detergents to maintain activity at higher temperature and pH.
2. Proteases and lipases derived from alkaliphilic bacteria used as detergent additives to increase stain removal.
3. Some archaea bear potential for bioremediation, cleaning contaminated sites.
4. Thermus aquaticus, a thermophile, is essential to molecular biology as the source of the enzyme (Taq polymerase) used to amplify DNA in the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR).
summary: This section defines Archaea and describes their general features, classification, and beneficial aspects. Archaeans, species in the Domain Archaea, are unicellular, microscopic organisms similar to bacteria that live as producers or decomposers. Their characteristics: prokaryotic, single-celled, lacking membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, lacking true peptidoglycan in cell walls, having branched hydrocarbon chains in their membrane lipids, and many are found in extreme environments. Three major physiological groups are recognized: methanogens (strictly anaerobic organisms that generate methane from organic molecules, found in waterlogged soils, lake and marine sediments, marshes, and animal GI tracts), extreme halophiles (grow in highly saline environments like the Great Salt Lake and Dead Sea; generally obligate aerobes), and extremely thermophilic Archaea/hyperthermophiles (found near volcanic vents, optimum temperatures over 80 degrees C, can be obligate/facultative aerobes or obligate anaerobes), plus thermophilic extreme acidophiles (Thermoplasma and Picrophilus growing in hot acidic environments). Archaea were identified as a distinct type of prokaryote by unique rRNA sequences; they are distinguished from bacteria by lack of true peptidoglycan, branched membrane lipids, and methionine (not N-formylmethionine) as the initial amino acid in polypeptides coded by the AUG start codon (as in eukaryotes). Archaea multiply by binary fission, budding, fragmentation, or other mechanisms. Beneficial uses: enzymes (proteases, lipases from alkaliphilic bacteria) as detergent additives that stay active at high temperature/pH; bioremediation potential; and Thermus aquaticus as the source of Taq polymerase enabling PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction).

notes:
Major Physical Factors Affecting Microbial Growth
- Solutes and water activity
- pH
- Temperature
- Oxygen level
- Pressure
- Radiation

Classes of Microbes Based on Temperature
- Psychrophiles (also called cryophiles): like it cold, e.g., one in the Antarctic grows best at 4 degrees C.
- Psychrotrophs: grow at lower but not extreme temperatures.
- Mesophiles: grow at moderate temperatures (optimum near body/household temperatures).
- Thermophiles: live at high temperatures.
- Hyperthermophiles: live at really high temperatures (present record is 121 degrees C).

Classes of Microbes Based on Salt / Salinity
- Halophiles: live in very saline environments (like the Dead Sea).
- Extreme halophiles: grow in highly saline environments.

Classes of Microbes Based on pH
- Acidophiles: live at low pH (as low as pH 1) and may die at pH 7.
- Alkaliphiles: live at high pH; their enzymes are used as detergent additives.

Classes of Microbes Based on Oxygen
- Aerobes: require oxygen.
- Facultative anaerobes: can grow with or without oxygen.
- Obligate anaerobes: cannot tolerate oxygen.

Practical Significance
- Understanding these factors is important for sterilization, food preservation, and growing microorganisms in the laboratory.
summary: The environments in which some microorganisms grow would kill most other microorganisms. The major physical factors that affect microbial growth are solutes and water activity, pH, temperature, oxygen level, pressure, and radiation. Microbes are classified by their temperature preference into psychrophiles (growing best in cold, e.g., ~4 degrees C in Antarctic), psychrotrophs, mesophiles (moderate temperatures, most common), thermophiles (high temperatures), and hyperthermophiles (very high temperatures, up to ~121 degrees C). They are further classified by oxygen requirement (aerobes, facultative anaerobes, anaerobes), by salinity (halophiles, e.g., Dead Sea organisms), and by pH (acidophiles living at low pH, as low as pH 1, who die at pH 7; alkaliphiles living at high pH).

notes:
Definition and Terminology
- Fungus (pl. fungi): eukaryotic organisms that are spore-bearing, have absorptive nutrition, lack chlorophyll, and reproduce sexually and asexually.
- Mycologist: scientist who studies fungi; Mycology: the discipline of studying fungi.
- Mycotoxicology: study of fungal toxins and their effects.
- Mycoses: diseases caused by fungi in animals (singular mycosis).

General Characteristics of True Fungi
1. All are eukaryotic (membrane-bound nuclei containing chromosomes, and membrane-bound cytoplasmic organelles such as mitochondria, vacuoles, ER).
2. Most are filamentous - composed of microscopic filaments called hyphae with apical growth, branching to form a network called a mycelium; hyphae may be septate or nonseptate (coenocytic).
3. Some are unicellular, e.g., yeasts.
4. Protoplasm is surrounded by a rigid wall composed primarily of chitin and glucans (walls of some species contain cellulose).
5. Many reproduce both sexually and asexually, often producing spores.
6. Nuclei are typically haploid and hyphal compartments often multinucleate (Oomycota and some yeasts have diploid nuclei).
7. All are achlorophyllous (lack chlorophyll) and incapable of photosynthesis.
8. All are chemoheterotrophic (chemoorganotrophic) - use pre-existing organic carbon sources and chemical reaction energy.
9. Possess a characteristic range of storage compounds (trehalose, glycogen, sugar alcohols, lipids).
10. Nutritionally categorized into three types: saprophytic, parasitic, and symbiotic.

Ecology of Fungi
- Colonized nearly all environments; frequently found in cool, dark, moist places with a supply of decaying material.
- Saprobes that decompose organic matter.
- Many establish mycorrhizal associations with plant roots; some ants farm fungi as food.
- Lichens: symbiotic relationship between a fungus and a photosynthetic organism (usually an alga or cyanobacterium); the photobiont provides energy from light and carbohydrates, the fungus supplies minerals and protection.
- Some animals that consume fungi help disseminate spores over long distances.

Classification of Fungi (5 major groups)
- Chytridiomycota: zoospore-producing fungi, e.g., Allomyces, water molds.
- Glomeromycota: e.g., mycorrhizal fungi.
- Zygomycota: sporangial fungi, e.g., Rhizopus, Mucor.
- Ascomycota: ascospore-producing fungi, e.g., Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
- Basidiomycota: basidia-producing fungi, e.g., rusts and smuts.

Reproduction in Fungi
Sporulation: process of spore formation in structures (fruiting bodies) from which spores are released.
A) Asexual reproduction:
- Asexual structures develop on specialized hyphae; mitotic divisions produce thousands of genetically identical spores.
- Sporangiospores: spores formed within sacs/vessels called sporangia (e.g., bread mold Rhizopus).
- Conidia: unprotected, dust-like spores produced on conidiophores (e.g., conidiophores and conidia).
- Arthrospores: spores formed by fragmentation of hyphae (fungi causing athlete's foot multiply this way).
- Budding in yeasts: cell becomes swollen at one edge, a new cell called a blastospore buds from the parent cell and breaks free; parent continues producing blastospores.
- Spores are extremely light and blown about in huge numbers by wind.
B) Sexual reproduction:
- Opposite mating types come together and fuse; because the nuclei are genetically different, the fusion cell is a heterokaryon (genetically dissimilar nuclei existing in a common cytoplasm).
- Nuclei fuse forming a diploid cell; chromosome number halved by meiosis, returning to haploid.
- A visible fruiting body (e.g., mushroom) often results and is the location of the haploid spores.

Economic Importance of Fungi
Beneficial aspects:
1. Saprobes/parasites decomposing complex organic substrates - essential for recycling carbon and other elements; decomposer activity is key to the cycle of life.
2. Edible wild or domesticated mushrooms (Basidiomycetes) are important food sources.
3. Yeasts are essential to industrial fermentation processes: bread, wine, beer.
4. Important in preparing cheeses, soy sauce, sufu, and Ethiopian traditional fermentations (Enjera, Tela/Farsoo, Tej/Dadhii, bulla).
5. Molds (e.g., Aspergillus species) produce commercial Organic acids: citric, oxalic, gluconic, itaconic, gallic acids, and drugs (ergometrine, cortisone); Fusarium produces 12-15 g fat per litre of 50% glucose solution within 48 hours - fermentation yields industrial alcohol, fats and proteins.
6. Major role in manufacture of antibiotics (penicillin, griseofulvin) and the immunosuppressive drug cyclosporin.
7. Actinomycetes and fungi are important sources of antibiotics: penicillin, amphotericin B, adriamycin, bleomycin.
8. Fungi are useful tools for studying complex eukaryotic events such as cancer and aging within a simple cell.

Harmful aspects of Fungi:
1. Major cause of plant diseases (invade leaves through stomates); over 5,000 species attack economically valuable crops, garden plants, and wild plants; also cause diseases of animals and humans.
2. Molds cause deterioration of fabrics, leather, electrical insulation, and other manufactured goods.
3. Fungi spoil improperly stored agricultural produce - vegetables, fruits, cereals.
4. Mycotoxicoses (ingestion of fungal toxins) and mycetismus (mushroom poisoning).
   - A. Aflatoxins: produced by Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus in warm humid climates contaminating peanuts, grains, cereals, sweet potatoes, corn, rice, and animal feed; thought to be carcinogenic, especially in the liver.
   - B. Ergotism: Claviceps purpurea (ascomycete) grows on rye, wheat, and barley kernels; dense tissue hardens into a sclerotium; alkaloids deposited in grain as ergot; bread from rye grain may cause ergotism (ergot rye disease).
   - C. Mushroom poisoning (mycetism): from mushrooms producing mycotoxins.
5. Superficial fungal infections: mycoses of the outermost areas - hair, nails, and dead outer skin layers (epidermis) - caused by Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, Microsporum; forms are tineas or 'ringworm': Tinea corporis (hairless skin), Tinea pedis/athlete's foot (lower legs), Tinea capitis (scalp, eyebrows, eyelashes), Tinea barbae (beard), Tinea unguium/onychomycosis (nails).
- Transmission: direct human contact, animal-human contact, or indirectly on inanimate objects (clothes, carpets, showers, swimming pools, gyms).
- Prevention: regular disinfection of showers and wardrobes, keeping skin dry, not sharing personal items.
- Other fungal diseases: Candidiasis (Candida albicans - itching, burning, cheesy discharge), Thrush (Candida albicans, white flecks on mucous membranes), Aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus - bloody cough, chest pain, wheezing, shortness of breath, airborne spores).
summary: Fungi are eukaryotic, spore-bearing organisms that lack chlorophyll, have absorptive nutrition, and reproduce sexually and asexually. Mycology is the scientific study of fungi; mycotoxicology studies fungal toxins; diseases caused by fungi in animals are mycoses. Ecology: fungi are found in cool, dark, moist places with decaying material; they are saprobes decomposing organic matter, form mycorrhizal associations with plant roots, lichens are symbiotic relationships between a fungus and a photosynthetic organism (alga or cyanobacterium). Classification: five major groups - Chytridiomycota (zoospore-producing), Glomeromycota (mycorrhizal), Zygomycota (sporangial, e.g., Rhizopus, Mucor), Ascomycota (ascospore-producing, e.g., Saccharomyces cerevisiae), Basidiomycota (basidia-producing, e.g., rusts and smuts). Reproduction: asexual reproduction via spores (sporangiospores in sporangia, conidia on conidiophores, arthrospores by fragmentation; yeast budding producing blastospores) and sexual reproduction involving fusion of opposite mating types forming heterokaryons and eventually diploid cells, with fruiting bodies such as mushrooms. Economic importance: beneficial (decomposition/recycling of carbon, edible mushrooms, fermentation for bread/wine/beer, preparation of cheeses, soy sauce, Ethiopian traditional fermentations like Enjera, Tela, Tej, bulla, commercial organic acids, antibiotics like penicillin and griseofulvin, drugs like cyclosporin, tools for studying cancer and aging) and harmful (plant diseases attacking leaves through stomates, deterioration of fabrics/leather/electrical insulation, spoilage of stored agricultural produce, mycotoxicoses including aflatoxins from Aspergillus flavus/parasiticus, ergotism from Claviceps purpurea, mushroom poisoning/mycetism, and superficial fungal infections such as tinea/ringworm and candidiasis).

10. Nutritionally categorized into three types: saprophytic, parasitic, and symbiotic.

notes:
Sporulation: the process of spore formation. It usually occurs in structures (fruiting bodies) that are part of the fungus in which spores are formed and from which they are released. These structures may be asexual (invisible to the naked eye) or sexual, such as macroscopic mushrooms.

A) Asexual Reproduction
- Asexual reproductive structures develop at the ends of specialized hyphae; as a result of mitotic divisions, thousands of spores are produced, all genetically identical.
- Sporangiospores: many asexual spores develop within sacs or vessels called sporangia (e.g., the bread mold Rhizopus).
- Conidia: other fungi produce spores on supportive structures called conidiophores; these unprotected, dust-like spores are known as conidia.
- Arthrospores: in some fungi, spores form simply by fragmentation of the hyphae (arthro='joint'); the fungi that cause athlete's foot multiply in this manner.
- Budding in yeasts: the cell becomes swollen at one edge and a new cell, called a blastospore, develops (buds) from the parent cell; eventually the spore breaks free to live independently, and the parent cell can continue producing additional blastospores.
- Fungal spores are extremely light and are blown about in huge numbers by wind currents.

B) Sexual Reproduction
- Many fungi produce spores by sexual reproduction. Opposite mating types come together and fuse.
- Because the nuclei are genetically different in each mating type, the fusion cell represents a heterokaryon (hetero='different', karyo='nucleus') - a cell with genetically dissimilar nuclei existing for some length of time in a common dikaryotic cytoplasm.
- Eventually the nuclei fuse and a diploid cell is formed.
- The chromosome number soon is halved by meiosis, returning the cell or organism to a haploid condition.
- A visible fruiting body often results during sexual reproduction and it is the location of the haploid spores; the most recognized fruiting body from which spores are produced is the mushroom.
summary: Fungal reproduction involves sporulation, the process of spore formation in structures from which spores are released; these may be asexual (invisible to the naked eye) or sexual such as macroscopic mushrooms. Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical spores at the ends of specialized hyphae by mitotic divisions; spores may form within sporangia (sporangiospores, e.g., bread mold Rhizopus), on conidiophores (conidia), or by fragmentation of hyphae (arthrospores, e.g., the fungi causing athlete's foot). Many yeasts reproduce asexually by budding, forming blastospores. Fungal spores are extremely light and blown about in huge numbers by wind. Sexual reproduction involves fusion of opposite mating types: because the nuclei are genetically different, the fusion cell is a heterokaryon with genetically dissimilar nuclei in a common dikaryotic cytoplasm; eventually nuclei fuse forming a diploid cell, whose chromosome number is halved by meiosis, returning to haploid. A visible fruiting body often results, the most recognizable being the mushroom, which is the location of haploid spores.

notes:
Beneficial Aspects of Fungi
1. Fungi exist as saprobes or parasites; their preeminent ability to break down complex organic substrates is essential for recycling carbon and other elements in the cycle of life.
2. Edible wild or domesticated varieties of mushrooms (Basidiomycetes) are important as food sources.
3. Fungi, especially the yeasts, are essential to industrial fermentation processes such as bread, wine, and beer.
4. Fungi play a major role in preparation of some cheeses, soy sauce, sufu, and Ethiopian traditional fermented products: Enjera, Tela (Farsoo), Tej (Dadhii), bulla, etc.
5. Molds (such as Aspergillus species) are used in production of Organic acids: citric, oxalic, gluconic, itaconic acid; and drugs: ergometrine, cortisone.
6. Fungi play a major role in manufacture of antibiotics (penicillin, griseofulvin) and the immunosuppressive drug cyclosporin.
7. Actinomycetes and fungi are important sources of antibiotics: penicillin, amphotericin B, adriamycin, bleomycin.
8. Fungi are useful tools for studying complex eukaryotic events, such as cancer and aging, within a simple cell.
- Products of fermentation yield industrial alcohol, fats, and proteins (e.g., the mold Fusarium can produce 12-15 g of fat per litre of 50% glucose solution within 48 hours).

Harmful Aspects of Fungi
1. Fungi are a major cause of plant diseases; they can invade leaves through stomates. Over 5,000 species attack economically valuable crops, garden plants, and many wild plants; fungi also cause many diseases of animals and humans.
2. Molds cause deterioration of fabrics, leather, electrical insulation, and other manufactured goods.
3. Fungi spoil agricultural produce if improperly stored - destroying vegetables, fruits, and cereals.
4. Mycotoxicoses (ingestion of toxins of fungal origin) and mycetismus (mushroom poisoning through ingestion of fungal elements):
   A. Aflatoxins: Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus produce mycotoxins called aflatoxins; molds are found in warm, humid climates contaminating peanuts, grains, cereals, sweet potatoes, corn, rice, and animal feed; aflatoxins are carcinogenic, especially in the liver; contaminated meat and dairy are sources.
   B. Ergotism: caused by Claviceps purpurea (ascomycete) producing alkaloids; grows on kernels of rye, wheat, barley; dense tissue hardens into a purple body called a sclerotium; bread made from rye grain may cause ergotism (ergot rye disease).
   C. Mushroom poisoning (mycetism): from mushrooms producing mycotoxins affecting the human body.
5. Superficial Fungal Infections (dermatophytoses): infections of the outermost areas of the body - hair, fingernails, toenails, dead outer skin layers (epidermis) - caused by filamentous fungi: Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, Microsporum.
   Forms (tineas / 'ringworm'): Tinea corporis (hairless skin; Microsporum canis, Trichophyton mentagrophytes); Tinea pedis/athlete's foot (lower legs; T. rubrum, T. mentagrophytes, Epidermophyton floccosum); Tinea capitis (scalp, eyebrows, eyelashes; T. tonsurans, M. canis); Tinea barbae (beard ringworm; T. rubrum, T. mentagrophytes); Tinea unguium/onychomycosis (nails; T. rubrum, T. mentagrophytes, E. floccosum).
   Transmission: directly by human contact, animal-human contact, or indirectly on inanimate objects (clothes, carpets, moisture, dust in showers, swimming pools, wardrobes, gyms).
   Prevention: regular disinfection of showers and wardrobes; keeping skin dry, not sharing personal items.

Summary Table of Fungal Diseases
- Dermatophytosis (tineas): Epidermophyton, Microsporum, Trichophyton; blister-like lesions of skin; spread via fragments on floors/surfaces; prevent by keeping skin dry and not sharing personal items.
- Candidiasis: Candida albicans; itching, burning pains, 'cheesy' discharge; sexually transmitted; avoid baths, tubs, douches.
- Thrush: Candida albicans; white flecks on mucous membranes; passes through the birth canal; practice good oral hygiene, limit sugar intake.
- Aspergillosis: Aspergillus fumigatus; bloody cough, chest pain, wheezing, shortness of breath; airborne spores; stay away from sources of mold.
