summary: This section discusses the shape of frequency distributions as represented by frequency curves. It explains how the relationship between the mean, median, and mode indicates the skewness of a distribution. A symmetrical distribution has mean = median = mode. A positively skewed distribution (skewed to the right) has mean > median > mode. A negatively skewed distribution (skewed to the left) has mean < median < mode. The section also introduces Pearson's and Bowley's coefficients of skewness as quantitative measures of skewness.
keywords:
• Skewness: A measure of the asymmetry of a distribution.
• Positively Skewed: A distribution with a longer tail on the right side; mean > median > mode.
• Negatively Skewed: A distribution with a longer tail on the left side; mean < median < mode.
• Symmetrical Distribution: A distribution where the mean, median, and mode are equal.
• Pearson's Coefficient of Skewness: A measure of skewness based on the mean, median, and standard deviation.
• Bowley's Coefficient of Skewness: A measure of skewness based on quartiles.

notes: A population is the entire group of individuals or items being studied. A sample is a subset of the population. Probability sampling methods ensure that every member of the population has a known, non-zero chance of being selected, allowing for unbiased inferences. Simple Random Sampling (SRS) is the most basic method, often implemented using a lottery or random number table. Systematic Sampling selects every kth item from a list. Stratified Sampling divides the population into homogeneous subgroups (strata) and samples from each. Cluster Sampling selects entire groups (clusters) at random. Multistage Sampling uses a combination of methods in stages. The choice of sampling technique depends on the population, resources, and objectives of the study. The section also briefly demonstrates how to compute range, variance, and standard deviation using Excel.
summary: This section introduces the concepts of population and sample in statistics. It explains the importance of sampling and describes different probability sampling techniques: simple random sampling (lottery method, random number table), systematic sampling, stratified sampling, cluster sampling, and multistage sampling. The advantages and limitations of each method are discussed. The section also provides a brief introduction to using Microsoft Excel for statistical calculations.
keywords:
• Population: The entire set of individuals or items of interest in a study.
• Sample: A subset of a population selected for study.
• Simple Random Sampling: A sampling method where each member of the population has an equal chance of being selected.
• Systematic Sampling: A sampling method where elements are selected from a list at regular intervals.
• Stratified Sampling: A sampling method where the population is divided into strata and a random sample is taken from each.
• Cluster Sampling: A sampling method where entire groups or clusters are randomly selected.
• Multistage Sampling: A complex sampling method involving sampling at multiple stages.
• Sampling Frame: A list of all individuals in the population from which a sample is drawn.

sub_section: Graphical Solutions of System of Linear Inequalities
notes: A linear inequality in one variable (e.g., ax + b < 0) can be solved algebraically. A linear inequality in two variables (e.g., ax + by < c) has a solution set consisting of all points that lie on one side of the corresponding boundary line (ax + by = c). This side is called a half-plane. To graph a linear inequality, first graph the boundary line. If the inequality is strict (< or >), the line is dashed (not included). If it is non-strict (≤ or ≥), the line is solid (included). Then, test a point (like (0,0)) to determine which half-plane satisfies the inequality and shade that region. The solution to a system of linear inequalities is the intersection of the solution regions of all inequalities in the system. This solution region, also called the feasible region, can be bounded or unbounded. The vertices (corner points) of this region are the intersection points of the boundary lines.
summary: This section covers the graphical solution of systems of linear inequalities. It begins with solving linear inequalities in one variable and then extends to two variables. The concept of a half-plane and the steps for graphing linear inequalities are explained. The solution region (feasible region) of a system of inequalities is the intersection of the half-planes that satisfy each inequality. The section also discusses the concept of a vertex (corner point) of the solution region.
keywords:
• Linear Inequality: An inequality that involves a linear expression.
• Half-Plane: One of the two regions into which a line divides a plane.
• System of Linear Inequalities: A set of two or more linear inequalities that must be satisfied simultaneously.
• Feasible Region: The set of all points that satisfy a system of linear inequalities.
• Vertex (Corner Point): A point of intersection of two or more boundary lines of a feasible region.

notes: A Linear Programming Problem (LPP) involves optimizing (maximizing or minimizing) a linear objective function subject to a set of linear constraints. The objective function is the function to be optimized (e.g., maximize profit Z = ax + by). Constraints are the inequalities that limit the values of the decision variables (x and y). The feasible region is the graphical representation of all points that satisfy all constraints. The Corner Point Theorem states that if an optimal solution exists, it will be found at a corner point (vertex) of the feasible region. The Corner Point Method involves the following steps: (1) Graph the feasible region. (2) Determine the coordinates of all corner points. (3) Evaluate the objective function at each corner point. (4) Choose the point that gives the maximum or minimum value. If the feasible region is unbounded, an optimal solution may not exist.
summary: This section introduces the fundamental concepts of linear programming. It defines the objective function, constraints, and feasible region. The key theorem is presented: the optimal value (maximum or minimum) of a linear objective function over a feasible region occurs at a vertex (corner point) of the region. The Corner Point Method is explained as a systematic way to find the optimal solution: graph the feasible region, find all corner points, evaluate the objective function at each corner point, and select the largest (for maximization) or smallest (for minimization) value. The section also covers the difference between bounded and unbounded feasible regions.
keywords:
• Linear Programming: A mathematical method for finding the maximum or minimum value of a linear function subject to linear constraints.
• Objective Function: The linear function to be maximized or minimized.
• Constraints: The linear inequalities that define the feasible region.
• Decision Variables: The variables (x and y) whose values determine the objective function.
• Optimal Solution: The point in the feasible region that gives the maximum or minimum value of the objective function.
• Bounded Feasible Region: A feasible region that can be enclosed within a finite area.
• Unbounded Feasible Region: A feasible region that extends infinitely in some direction.
• Corner Point Method: A method for solving an LP problem by evaluating the objective function at all vertices of the feasible region.

notes: Linear programming is widely used to solve practical problems in various fields. Diet Problems involve minimizing the cost of a diet subject to nutritional constraints. Manufacturing Problems involve maximizing profit subject to constraints on resources like labor, materials, and machine time. Allocation Problems involve allocating scarce resources to optimize a certain objective, such as minimizing the intake of a harmful substance. Transportation Problems involve minimizing the cost of transporting goods from supply points to demand points. The process of formulating an LP problem involves identifying the decision variables, writing the objective function, and writing the constraints. For more complex problems with multiple variables, a spreadsheet tool like Microsoft Excel Solver can be used to find the optimal solution by specifying the objective cell, changing cells (variables), and constraints.
summary: This section presents real-world applications of linear programming. It covers diet problems, manufacturing problems, allocation problems, and transportation problems. Each type of problem requires formulating the objective function and constraints based on the given scenario. The section also includes a guide on using Microsoft Excel's Solver tool to solve linear programming problems, which is useful for problems with more than two variables where the graphical method is not practical.
keywords:
• Diet Problem: An LP problem to find the minimum-cost diet that meets nutritional requirements.
• Manufacturing Problem: An LP problem to maximize profit or minimize cost in production.
• Allocation Problem: An LP problem to allocate resources to optimize an objective.
• Transportation Problem: An LP problem to minimize the cost of transporting goods.
• Excel Solver: An optimization tool in Microsoft Excel for solving linear programming problems.

notes: A ratio is a comparison of two quantities of the same kind. It is represented as a:b or a/b. The terms of a ratio (a and b) must be in the same units. A part-to-whole ratio compares a part of a group to the whole group. A part-to-part ratio compares two parts of a group. Equivalent ratios are obtained by multiplying or dividing both terms of a ratio by the same non-zero number. A continued ratio compares three or more quantities, such as a:b:c. To allocate an amount in a given ratio, divide the total amount by the sum of the ratio terms to find the value of one part, then multiply each term by this value.
summary: This section defines a ratio as a comparison of two numbers by division. It covers the notation for ratios (a:b or a/b) and the importance of expressing quantities in the same units before finding the ratio. The distinction between part-to-whole and part-to-part ratios is made. Equivalent ratios are introduced, and the concept of a continued ratio (comparing three or more quantities) is explained. Practical examples of allocating amounts in a given ratio are also provided.
keywords:
• Ratio: A comparison of two numbers by division.
• Part-to-Whole Ratio: A ratio comparing a part of a group to the whole group.
• Part-to-Part Ratio: A ratio comparing two parts of a group.
• Continued Ratio: A ratio comparing three or more quantities.
• Equivalent Ratios: Ratios that represent the same comparison.

notes: A rate is similar to a ratio but compares quantities with different units, such as speed (kilometers per hour) or price (Birr per kilogram). A unit rate has a denominator of 1 (e.g., 60 km/h). The rate of change is defined as (Final Amount - Original Amount) / Original Amount. A positive rate of change indicates an increase, while a negative rate indicates a decrease. Average rate of change is used to describe how a quantity changes on average over a period. In business, rates are used to describe costs, productivity, and growth.
summary: This section defines a rate as a ratio comparing two quantities with different units. It introduces the concept of a unit rate (a rate with a denominator of 1). The rate of change is defined as the change in a quantity relative to the original amount, which can be positive (increase) or negative (decrease). Examples of rates in business and everyday life are provided.
keywords:
• Rate: A comparison of two quantities with different units.
• Unit Rate: A rate with a denominator of 1.
• Unit Price: The cost of one unit of an item, a type of unit rate.
• Rate of Change: The ratio of the change in a quantity to its original amount.

notes: A proportion is an equation of two equal ratios: a:b = c:d (or a/b = c/d). In the proportion a/b = c/d, the terms a and d are the extremes, and b and c are the means. The fundamental property is ad = bc. Direct proportion: Two quantities x and y are directly proportional if their ratio is constant (y = kx). Inverse proportion: Two quantities are inversely proportional if their product is constant (xy = k). Compound proportion (joint variation) occurs when one variable is proportional to the product of two or more other variables. These concepts are essential for solving problems involving scaling, rates, and relationships between variables.
summary: This section defines a proportion as an equation stating that two ratios are equal. The terms of a proportion are explained: the extremes (first and last terms) and the means (second and third terms). The key property that the product of the means equals the product of the extremes (cross-multiplication) is stated. The concept of direct proportion (x ∝ y), inverse proportion (x ∝ 1/y), and compound proportion (joint variation) are introduced.
keywords:
• Proportion: An equation that states two ratios are equal.
• Extremes: The first and last terms in a proportion (a and d in a:b = c:d).
• Means: The second and third terms in a proportion (b and c in a:b = c:d).
• Direct Proportion: A relationship where two quantities increase or decrease together at a constant ratio.
• Inverse Proportion: A relationship where one quantity increases as the other decreases, and vice versa.
• Compound Proportion: A situation where one quantity depends on two or more other quantities.

notes: A percentage is a number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100. The basic relationship is: Part = Whole × Rate, or Percentage = Base × Rate. Markup is the amount added to the cost of a product to determine its selling price: Markup = Selling Price - Cost. Markup rate can be expressed as a percentage of cost or selling price: Markup Rate (on cost) = Markup / Cost × 100%; Markup Rate (on selling price) = Markup / Selling Price × 100%. A discount is a reduction from the regular price: Discount = Regular Price - Sale Price. The discount rate is Discount / Regular Price × 100%. Percentages are widely used in business for calculating taxes, profits, interest, and discounts.
summary: This section covers the concept of percentage, which is a ratio expressed as a fraction of 100. It explains the relationship between the base, rate, and percentage (Percentage = Base × Rate). The section also discusses practical applications of percentages, including markup (the difference between selling price and cost) and discount (a reduction in the regular price). Formulas for markup rate and discount rate are provided.
keywords:
• Percentage: A number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100.
• Base: The whole amount to which a percentage is applied.
• Rate: The percentage expressed as a decimal or fraction.
• Markup: The difference between the selling price and the cost of an item.
• Discount: A reduction in the regular price of an item.

notes: Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal. The formula is I = P × r × t, where I is interest, P is principal, r is the annual interest rate (as a decimal), and t is time in years. The total amount to be repaid (future value) is A = P + I = P(1 + rt). Key terms: Principal (the amount borrowed or invested), Interest (the cost of borrowing money), Rate (the percentage charged per year), Term (the duration of the loan). Simple interest is rarely used in modern banking but is a foundational concept. Formulas for finding other variables: P = I/(rt), r = I/(Pt), t = I/(Pr).
summary: This section introduces simple interest, which is computed only on the principal amount. The simple interest formula is I = Prt, where P is the principal, r is the annual interest rate, and t is the time in years. The future value (amount) is A = P + I = P(1 + rt). The section also explains related terms like debtor, creditor, and term of a loan. Examples show how to calculate interest, future value, principal, rate, and time.
keywords:
• Simple Interest: Interest computed only on the principal amount.
• Principal (P): The original amount of money invested or borrowed.
• Interest Rate (r): The percentage of the principal charged as interest per time period.
• Term (t): The duration of a loan or investment.
• Future Value (A): The total amount of money accumulated after a period, including principal and interest.

notes: Compound interest is interest calculated on the initial principal and also on the accumulated interest of previous periods. The future value is found using A = P(1 + i)^n, where n = m × t is the total number of compounding periods, and i = r/m is the interest rate per period. The effective interest rate (EAR) is the simple annual interest rate that would produce the same amount of interest as the compounding at a given frequency. It is calculated as EAR = (1 + r/m)^m - 1. More frequent compounding leads to a higher effective rate. Compound interest is the standard method used by financial institutions.
summary: This section introduces compound interest, where interest is earned on both the principal and the accumulated interest. The compound interest formula is A = P(1 + i)^(mt), where i = r/m is the interest rate per compounding period, m is the number of compounding periods per year, and t is the number of years. The section also covers the effective interest rate, which is the annually compounded rate equivalent to a given nominal rate and compounding frequency. The formula for the effective rate is EAR = (1 + r/m)^m - 1.
keywords:
• Compound Interest: Interest calculated on the initial principal and the accumulated interest from previous periods.
• Compounding Period: The time interval between interest calculations (e.g., annually, semi-annually, monthly).
• Nominal Interest Rate: The stated annual interest rate without considering compounding.
• Effective Interest Rate (EAR): The annual interest rate that accounts for the effect of compounding.

notes: An annuity is a stream of equal payments at regular intervals. An ordinary annuity has payments at the end of each period, while an annuity due has payments at the beginning. The future value of an ordinary annuity is FV = R × S_{n|i}, where R is the periodic payment, and S_{n|i} = ((1+i)^n - 1)/i is the future value annuity factor. The future value of an annuity due is FV = R × S_{n|i} × (1+i). The present value of an ordinary annuity is PV = R × a_{n|i}, where a_{n|i} = S_{n|i} / (1+i)^n = (1 - (1+i)^(-n))/i is the present value annuity factor. An annuity can be used to accumulate a future sum (savings) or to amortize a loan (mortgage).
summary: This section defines an annuity as a series of equal payments made at regular time intervals. It distinguishes between ordinary annuities (payments at the end of each period) and annuities due (payments at the beginning). The formulas for the future value of both types are provided. The present value of an ordinary annuity is also discussed, with formulas for the present value annuity factor. The concept is applied to calculating regular payments for loans (amortization).
keywords:
• Annuity: A series of equal payments made at regular intervals.
• Ordinary Annuity: An annuity with payments at the end of each period.
• Annuity Due: An annuity with payments at the beginning of each period.
• Future Value Annuity Factor (S_{n|i}): The future value of an ordinary annuity with a periodic payment of 1.
• Present Value Annuity Factor (a_{n|i}): The present value of an ordinary annuity with a periodic payment of 1.

notes: Amortization is the gradual repayment of a loan over a period through regular payments, which cover both interest and principal. An amortization schedule details each payment, showing the amount applied to interest, the amount applied to the principal, and the remaining balance. The payment amount R for a loan with principal PV, interest rate per period i, and number of payments n is found from the present value of an annuity formula: PV = R × a_{n|i}, so R = PV / a_{n|i}. In the early stages of a loan, the interest portion of the payment is high because the outstanding balance is large. As the balance decreases, the interest portion decreases, and the principal portion increases.
summary: This section explains amortization, the process of paying off a debt with regular payments over time. An amortization schedule shows the breakdown of each payment into interest and principal components. The formula for calculating the payment amount on a loan is derived from the present value of an annuity. The section highlights key points about amortization: early payments are mostly interest, and the portion going to principal increases over time.
keywords:
• Amortization: The process of paying off a debt with regular payments over time.
• Amortization Schedule: A table showing the breakdown of each loan payment into interest and principal.
• Payment to Principal: The portion of a loan payment that reduces the outstanding principal balance.

notes: Depreciation is the decrease in the value of an asset over time due to wear and tear or obsolescence. Appreciation is the increase in value. The declining balance method applies a fixed percentage rate to the asset's current value each year: Value at time n = Initial Value × (1 - Rate)^n. The straight-line method depreciates the asset by a fixed amount each year, calculated as (Initial Cost - Residual Value) / Useful Life. The value after t years is Initial Cost - (Annual Depreciation × t). The straight-line method results in a constant linear decline, while the declining balance method results in a larger depreciation in the early years that decreases over time.
summary: This section covers depreciation, the decline in the cash value of an asset over time. Two methods are discussed: declining balance depreciation (a fixed percentage of the current value) and straight-line depreciation (a fixed annual amount). The formulas for each method are provided, and the differences between them are compared. Examples include calculating the depreciated value of assets like cars and equipment.
keywords:
• Depreciation: A decrease in the value of an asset over time.
• Appreciation: An increase in the value of an asset over time.
• Declining Balance Depreciation: A depreciation method where a fixed percentage is applied to the current value of the asset.
• Straight-Line Depreciation: A depreciation method where a fixed amount of the asset's value is deducted each year.
• Residual Value (Salvage Value): The estimated value of an asset at the end of its useful life.
• Useful Life: The expected period of time during which an asset will be usable.

notes: Money functions as a medium of exchange, a store of value, and a unit of account. Saving is setting aside money for future use, typically in low-risk accounts. Investing involves purchasing assets (stocks, bonds, real estate) with the expectation of earning a return, but with higher risk. Savings institutions include commercial banks, savings and loan associations, and credit unions. Stocks represent ownership in a company and provide rights like voting and dividends. Bonds are debt instruments where the investor lends money to the issuer. Mutual funds pool money from many investors to invest in a diversified portfolio. Return on Investment (ROI) is a measure of profitability: ROI = (Current Value - Cost) / Cost × 100%. Financing can be obtained through equity (selling shares) or debt (borrowing money). Equity financing involves sharing ownership and profits, while debt financing involves paying interest and repaying the principal.
summary: This section discusses the fundamental concepts of personal and business finance. It defines money and its functions (medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account). It covers saving (low-risk, accessible) and investing (higher risk, potential for higher returns) and the reasons for each. It describes different saving institutions (commercial banks, saving and loan associations, credit unions). The section also introduces investment types: stocks (equity), bonds (debt), and mutual funds. It explains return on investment (ROI). Finally, it covers financing options: equity financing (selling ownership) and debt financing (borrowing).
keywords:

notes: Taxation is a compulsory financial charge imposed by the government to fund public expenditures. Direct taxes (e.g., income tax) are paid directly by the individual or business, while indirect taxes (e.g., VAT) are passed on to consumers. In Ethiopia, income tax is levied under four schedules: Schedule A (Employment Income) uses a progressive rate structure with tax brackets. Schedule B (Income from Rental of Buildings) taxes rental income after allowable deductions. Schedule C (Business Income) taxes business profits, with rates depending on the business category (A, B, or C). Schedule D (Other Incomes) covers royalties, dividends, interest, and other sources. Indirect taxes include Value Added Tax (VAT, 15% on most goods), Turnover Tax (2% on goods, 10% on services), Excise Tax (on specific goods like luxury items and alcohol), Customs Duty (on imports), and Stamp Duty (on legal instruments).
summary: This section provides an overview of taxation in Ethiopia. It explains the objectives and principles of taxation, and distinguishes between direct and indirect taxes. The section details the main schedules of income tax under Ethiopian law: Schedule 'A' (Employment Income), Schedule 'B' (Income from Rental of Buildings), Schedule 'C' (Business Income), and Schedule 'D' (Other Incomes). The tax rates and calculation methods (progression and deduction) for each schedule are described. The section also covers indirect taxes, including Value Added Tax (VAT), Turnover Tax, Excise Tax, Customs Duty, and Stamp Duty.

• Indirect Tax: A tax collected by an intermediary and passed on to the final consumer.
• Income Tax: A direct tax on the income of individuals and businesses.
• Value Added Tax (VAT): An indirect tax on the value added to a product at each stage of production and distribution.

notes:
--- Physics and geology ---

Physics and geology is the application of physics principles to study the Earth, its materials, and the processes that shape it. Physics is fundamental to understanding: Geophysics uses concepts like gravity, magnetism, seismology, and electrical conductivity to explore the Earth's subsurface structure, from its crust to its core. Plate Tectonics relies on fluid dynamics and heat transfer (convection) to explain the movement of tectonic plates. Mineral and Rock Physics uses principles of thermodynamics and material science to study the physical properties of minerals under high pressure and temperature. Dating Methods utilize nuclear physics (radioactivity and half-life) for radiometric dating of rocks and geological events. Physics provides the tools and conceptual framework to analyze seismic waves, measure magnetic fields, and understand the flow of matter deep within the Earth.

--- Physics and biology ---

To understand how life works, understanding physics is essential. Physics can explain the human body, covering: Mechanics of human motion , energetics of metabolism , fluid dynamics of blood flow , mechanisms for speaking and hearing , and the optical imaging system of the eye. Physics of Newtonian mechanics and biology: Newtonian mechanics explains how animals and their body parts move. Combined knowledge of physics and biology helps explain motion, such as why athletes and cheetahs run fast. Stability under gravity is governed by the principle that a body is in stable equilibrium if its center of mass (c.g.) is directly over its base of support. When the center of mass is outside the base, the torque from the weight tends to make the body fall. A person falls when their center of gravity is displaced beyond the feet's position. The wider the base and the closer the center of gravity is to the base, the more stable the body is. This also explains how we use our limbs. (See Figure 1.1 on page 9 for an illustration of a person's center of gravity and standing with an unbalanced load). Physics of fluid flow and biology: The physics of fluid flow (viscosity, equation of continuity, turbulent flow) is important for understanding blood circulation and blood pressure. Soft-bodied animals like the sea anemone and the earthworm use Pascal's principle for body motion (locomotion). Physics of sound wave and biology: Sound is a mechanical wave produced by vibrating bodies. In humans, the vocal cords produce sound when they come together and vibrate as air passes through them during exhalation. This vibration disturbs surrounding air molecules, transferring the motion and causing a vibrational disturbance (sound wave) to propagate. When the air vibrations reach the ear, they cause the eardrum to vibrate. (See Figure 1.2 on page 10 for an image of the vocal cords).

--- Physics and astronomy ---

Physics and astronomy is the study of the universe beyond Earth, applying fundamental physical laws to celestial objects, space, and time. Astronomy is essentially applied physics on a cosmic scale. Physics is crucial for understanding: Celestial Mechanics uses Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation to explain the orbits and motion of planets, stars, and galaxies. Astrophysics applies principles of thermodynamics, electromagnetism, and nuclear physics to study the life cycles (birth, evolution, and death) of stars, including concepts like nuclear fusion. Cosmology uses Einstein's Theory of Relativity and quantum mechanics to study the origin, large-scale structure, and fate of the entire universe (e.g., the Big Bang theory, dark matter, and dark energy). Spectroscopy (from atomic physics) is used to analyze the light emitted by stars and galaxies, determining their composition, temperature, and motion (using the Doppler effect).

--- Physics and chemistry ---

Physics is the most essential field of science and has a strong influence on most scientific developments. Concepts of physics are found in many modern sciences. Physics and chemistry overlap when the system under study involves matter composed of electrons and nuclei. Fundamental laws governing the behavior of matter apply to both. Both disciplines are concerned with matter and its interaction with energy. Atomic and subatomic particle physics explains the theory and rules about atoms important in chemistry. This physics is critically important for understanding how individual atoms join by covalent bonds to form molecules. It also provides quantitative insight into ionic and covalent bonding processes, showing which molecules are energetically favorable and the magnitudes of energies involved. The physics of energy related to heat tells chemists if a particular reaction is energetically possible and gives the reaction system's composition at equilibrium. The physics of heat energy provides a bridge between the macroscopic properties of a substance and the individual properties of its constituent molecules and atoms. Spectroscopy is the study of the interaction between matter and electromagnetic radiation as a function of wavelength or frequency. It is a fundamental examining tool in physics and chemistry, and most knowledge about the structure of atoms and molecules comes from spectroscopic study. Spectroscopic techniques are developed through the collaborative work of physicists and chemists. In general, the study of matter and electricity in physics is fundamental to understanding chemistry concepts like atomic structure, molecular structure, X-ray diffractions, radioactivity, periodic properties of elements, nature of valency, chemical bonds, and crystal structure of solids. Chemistry is rooted in atomic and molecular physics.

notes: Physics generates the foundational knowledge that is essential for all engineering disciplines. Civil engineering applies the laws of physics, particularly mechanics (forces, tension, elasticity) and fluid mechanics, to design and construct buildings, bridges, dams, and transportation systems. Mechanical engineering utilizes concepts such as mechanics, dynamics, thermodynamics, and materials science to create engines, vehicles, aircraft, and various mechanical systems. Electrical engineering is fundamentally based on the principles of electromagnetism and electricity for designing circuits, motors, and communication systems. Chemical engineering applies principles from molecular physics and thermodynamics to design and operate chemical processes for producing various materials. The relationship between physics and technology is reciprocal. While physics provides the basis for new technologies, technological advancements also enable new physics discoveries. For example, rocket technology allows for space-based experiments, and the development of X-ray technology advanced the study of atomic structure. This cycle of discovery and application is crucial for progress in both fields.
summary: This section describes the application of physics in various branches of engineering. It emphasizes that physics provides the fundamental knowledge needed for engineering disciplines. Civil engineering uses physics concepts like forces, fluid pressure, and gravity for designing and building infrastructure. Mechanical engineering relies on mechanics, thermodynamics, and dynamics for designing mechanical systems. Electrical engineering is based on electromagnetism, while chemical engineering requires knowledge of molecular physics and thermodynamics. The section also highlights the symbiotic relationship between physics and technology, where technological advancements (e.g., rocket technology, X-rays) enable further scientific discovery, completing a cycle of interdependence.

• Electrical Engineering: A branch of engineering that deals with the study and application of electricity, electronics, and electromagnetism.
• Chemical Engineering: A branch of engineering that applies chemistry, physics, and biology to design and operate processes that convert raw materials into valuable products.

notes: Medical physics is a branch of physics that applies the principles of physics to medicine, particularly for diagnosis and treatment. The discovery of X-rays in 1895 was a pivotal moment that led to the development of medical imaging. MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) uses the magnetic properties of protons (hydrogen nuclei) within the body. When placed in a strong magnetic field, these protons align. A radiofrequency pulse disrupts this alignment, and as they relax back, they release energy. Different tissues emit different amounts of energy, which is detected and processed by a computer to create detailed images of soft tissues. CT (Computed Tomography) scan uses a rotating X-ray source and detectors to take multiple X-ray images from different angles. A computer combines these images to create cross-sectional 'slices' of the body, providing more detailed information than a standard X-ray. Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves (above 20 kHz). A transducer emits sound waves into the body, and the reflected echoes are detected to create an image. The appearance of tissues is described as anechoic (no echoes, fluid-filled), hypoechoic (few echoes), or hyperechoic (many echoes). The stethoscope is a simple acoustic device used to listen to internal body sounds (heart, lungs). Radiation therapy uses high-energy radiation (X-rays, gamma rays, or particle beams) to destroy cancer cells. The radiation damages the DNA of rapidly dividing cancer cells. The treatment is often targeted to minimize damage to surrounding healthy tissue, sometimes using external beams or implanted radioactive sources.
summary: This section discusses the application of physics principles in medicine for diagnosis and treatment. It covers the foundational discovery of X-rays and its impact. The section details the principles and working mechanisms of several key medical imaging technologies: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), which uses the magnetic properties of hydrogen protons to generate detailed images of soft tissues; X-ray Computed Tomography (CT), which uses rotating X-ray beams to produce cross-sectional images; and Ultrasound, which uses high-frequency sound waves to visualize body structures. It also explains the clinical use of the stethoscope and the therapeutic application of radiation (Radiation Therapy) for treating cancer.
keywords:
• Medical Imaging: Technologies used to view the human body for the purpose of diagnosing, monitoring, or treating medical conditions.
• Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI): A medical imaging technique that uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to generate detailed images of the body's soft tissues.
• Computed Tomography (CT) Scan: A medical imaging technique that uses rotating X-ray beams to create cross-sectional images of the body.
• Ultrasound: A medical imaging technique that uses high-frequency sound waves to visualize internal body structures.
• Anechoic: An area on an ultrasound image that appears black because it does not reflect sound waves, typically indicating a fluid-filled region.
• Hyperechoic: An area on an ultrasound image that appears light gray because it reflects many sound waves.
• Hypoechoic: An area on an ultrasound image that appears dark gray because it reflects few sound waves.
• Radiation Therapy: The use of high-energy radiation to treat cancer by destroying the DNA of cancer cells.
• Stethoscope: A medical instrument used for listening to sounds produced within the body, such as heart and lung sounds.

notes: Physics is fundamental to the development of modern defense technologies. Radar (Radio Detection And Ranging) uses electromagnetic waves to detect and track objects like aircraft, ships, and missiles. It works by transmitting a radio signal and analyzing the echo reflected from the target to determine its range and location. Missiles are projectile weapons guided by principles of mechanics (rocket propulsion, aerodynamics) and electronics. Ballistic missiles are rocket-powered initially and then follow a ballistic trajectory, while cruise missiles are jet-powered throughout their flight. Infrared (IR) detection is used for night vision and target acquisition. All objects emit infrared radiation based on their temperature (thermal radiation). IR devices, such as night vision goggles, detect these temperature differences to create an image, allowing vision in the absence of visible light. Other defense applications include laser guidance, satellite technology, and underwater acoustics for the navy.
summary: This section explains the critical role of physics in modern defense technology. It highlights that branches of the military (Air Force, Army, Navy, Space Force) rely on physics for various applications. The section focuses on three key areas: Radar technology, which uses radio waves to detect and track objects; Missiles, which are guided by Newtonian mechanics and electronic systems; and Infrared (IR) detection, which uses heat signatures for night vision and target acquisition. The underlying physics principles for these technologies include electromagnetism, optics, and mechanics.
keywords:
• Radar: An acronym for Radio Detection And Ranging; a system that uses radio waves to detect and locate objects.
• Missile: A rocket-propelled or jet-propelled weapon designed to deliver an explosive warhead to a target with high accuracy.
• Ballistic Missile: A missile that is rocket-powered in its initial phase and then follows a ballistic trajectory influenced only by gravity and air resistance.
• Cruise Missile: A jet-propelled missile that is powered throughout its flight and flies at a relatively low altitude.
• Infrared (IR) Detection: A technology that detects infrared radiation (heat) emitted by objects to create an image, used for night vision and target acquisition.
• Night Vision Goggles: Devices that use infrared detection or image intensification to allow vision in low-light conditions.

notes: A projectile is an object whose motion is governed solely by the force of gravity after its initial launch. Its trajectory is a parabola. The analysis of projectile motion relies on three key assumptions: (1) the acceleration due to gravity is constant and directed downward, (2) air resistance is negligible, and (3) horizontal velocity is constant because there is no horizontal acceleration. The motion is broken down into independent horizontal and vertical components, with time as the common linking variable. For horizontal projection (launched horizontally from a height), the initial vertical velocity is zero. The horizontal displacement is given by Δx = v0x * t, and the vertical displacement is Δy = (1/2)gt^2. The time of flight is determined solely by the height, t = sqrt(2Δy/g). The range is then R = v0x * sqrt(2Δy/g). For inclined projectile motion (launched at an angle θ with velocity v0), the initial velocity components are v0x = v0 cos θ and v0y = v0 sin θ. The horizontal velocity is constant (vx = v0 cos θ), and the vertical velocity changes as vy = v0 sin θ + gt. Displacements are Δx = v0 cos θ * t and Δy = v0 sin θ * t + (1/2)gt^2. The time to reach maximum height is t = v0 sin θ / g. The total time of flight (for launch and landing at the same height) is t_total = 2v0 sin θ / g. The maximum height H = (v0^2 sin^2 θ) / 2g. The horizontal range R = (v0^2 sin 2θ) / g. The range is maximum at θ = 45°. The relation between range and maximum height is H = (R tan θ)/4.
summary: This section covers the kinematics of projectile motion, which is the motion of an object under the sole influence of gravity. It establishes that projectile motion can be analyzed as two independent components: horizontal motion (constant velocity, no acceleration) and vertical motion (constant acceleration due to gravity). The section derives the key equations for horizontal and vertical displacement and velocity. It specifically addresses two cases: horizontal projection (from a height) and inclined projection (launched at an angle). For inclined projection, it derives equations for time of flight, maximum height, and horizontal range. It also discusses the relationship between range and maximum height, highlighting that the range is maximized at a 45-degree launch angle (assuming no air resistance).
keywords:
• Projectile: An object that is launched and moves only under the influence of gravity.
• Trajectory: The path followed by a projectile; a parabola in the absence of air resistance.
• Horizontal Projection: Projectile motion where the object is launched horizontally from a height.
• Inclined Projection: Projectile motion where the object is launched at an angle to the horizontal.
• Time of Flight: The total time a projectile spends in the air.
• Range: The maximum horizontal distance a projectile travels.
• Maximum Height: The highest vertical position reached by a projectile.

notes: Rotational motion is the motion of an object in a circle around a fixed axis. A rigid body is an object with a fixed shape where the distance between any two points remains constant. Angular displacement (Δθ) is the change in the angle of rotation, measured in radians. One complete revolution is 2π radians. Angular velocity (ω) is the rate of change of angular displacement, given by ω_av = Δθ/Δt, with units of rad/s. Angular acceleration (α) is the rate of change of angular velocity, given by α = Δω/Δt, with units of rad/s². The direction of ω and α is along the axis of rotation, determined by the right-hand rule: curling fingers in the direction of rotation gives the direction of ω with the thumb. For constant angular acceleration, the kinematic equations are: ω_f = ω_0 + αΔt, Δθ = ω_0Δt + (1/2)αΔt², and ω_f² = ω_0² + 2αΔθ. The relationships between angular and linear quantities for a point at a distance r from the axis are: s = rΔθ (arc length), v = rω (tangential speed), and a = rα (tangential acceleration). The linear speed is greater for points farther from the axis of rotation, although all points share the same angular speed.
summary: This section introduces the kinematics of rotational motion for a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis. It defines key angular quantities analogous to linear motion: angular displacement (Δθ), angular velocity (ω), and angular acceleration (α). The relationships between these angular quantities and their linear counterparts (tangential displacement s, tangential speed v, and tangential acceleration a) for a point on the rotating body are established as s = rθ, v = rω, and a = rα. The section also presents the equations of rotational kinematics for constant angular acceleration and provides a table comparing them to the linear equations of motion. The right-hand rule is described for determining the direction of angular velocity and acceleration.
keywords:
• Rotational Motion: The motion of an object in a circle around a fixed axis.
• Rigid Body: An object with a fixed shape and a constant distance between any two of its points.
• Angular Displacement: The change in the angle of rotation of an object.
• Angular Velocity: The rate of change of angular displacement of a rotating object.
• Angular Acceleration: The rate of change of angular velocity of a rotating object.
• Radian: The SI unit of angular measurement, where one revolution equals 2π radians.
• Right-Hand Rule: A rule used to determine the direction of the angular velocity vector; curling fingers in the direction of rotation gives the direction of ω with the thumb.
• Tangential Speed: The linear speed of a point on a rotating object, given by v = rω.
• Tangential Acceleration: The linear acceleration of a point on a rotating object, given by a = rα.

notes: Torque (τ) is the measure of the force's ability to cause rotational motion. It depends on the magnitude of the force, the distance from the axis of rotation to where the force is applied, and the angle between the force vector and the lever arm. The magnitude of torque is given by τ = rF sinθ. Its SI unit is Newton-meter (Nm), and its direction is along the axis of rotation. The moment of inertia (I) is the rotational analog of mass. It quantifies an object's resistance to changes in its rotational motion. It depends on the mass distribution of the object relative to the axis of rotation. For a point mass, I = mr². For a system of particles, I = Σ m_i r_i². The rotational analog of Newton's second law (F = ma) is τ_net = Iα, which states that the net torque on an object is equal to its moment of inertia times its angular acceleration.
summary: This section covers the dynamics of rotational motion, introducing the concepts of torque and moment of inertia. Torque is defined as the rotational effect of a force, given by τ = rF sinθ. It is the analog of force in linear motion and causes angular acceleration. The moment of inertia (I) is defined as the rotational inertia of an object, representing its resistance to changes in angular velocity. For a system of point masses, I = Σ m_i r_i². The rotational analog of Newton's second law is established as τ_net = Iα. Sample problems demonstrate how to calculate net torque, moment of inertia, and the resulting angular acceleration.
keywords:
• Torque: The rotational effect of a force, causing an object to acquire angular acceleration.
• Moment of Inertia: The quantitative measure of an object's rotational inertia; its resistance to changes in angular velocity.
• Axis of Rotation: The imaginary line around which an object rotates.

notes: Kepler's laws were derived from extensive astronomical observations made by Tycho Brahe. The First Law: The orbit of each planet is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. An ellipse is a closed curve where the sum of the distances from any point on the curve to the two foci is constant. The Second Law: A line joining the planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time. This implies that a planet's orbital speed is not constant; it is fastest at perihelion (closest to the Sun) and slowest at aphelion (farthest from the Sun). The Third Law: The square of the orbital period (T) of a planet is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis (average distance, R) of its orbit. Mathematically, T² ∝ R³, or T²/R³ = K. The constant K is approximately the same for all planets in our solar system. This law links the time it takes for a planet to orbit the Sun to its distance from the Sun.
summary: This section presents Kepler's three laws of planetary motion, which describe the orbits of planets around the Sun. Kepler's First Law (Law of Ellipses) states that planets orbit the Sun in elliptical paths with the Sun at one focus. Kepler's Second Law (Law of Equal Areas) states that an imaginary line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, meaning planets move faster when closer to the Sun (perihelion) and slower when farther (aphelion). Kepler's Third Law (Law of Harmonies) states that the square of a planet's orbital period (T) is proportional to the cube of its average orbital radius (R), or T²/R³ = K, where K is a constant for all planets orbiting the Sun.
keywords:
• Kepler's First Law: The orbit of a planet around the Sun is an ellipse with the Sun at one of the foci.
• Kepler's Second Law: A line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times.
• Kepler's Third Law: The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit (T² ∝ R³).
• Ellipse: An oval-shaped closed curve. The orbit of a planet is an ellipse.
• Focus (Foci): One of the two fixed points inside an ellipse. The Sun is at one focus of a planet's orbit.
• Perihelion: The point in a planet's orbit where it is closest to the Sun.
• Aphelion: The point in a planet's orbit where it is farthest from the Sun.
• Orbital Period: The time it takes for a planet or other object to complete one full orbit around another object.

notes: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation is a fundamental law of physics. It states that the force of gravity (F_g) between two objects is attractive and acts along the line connecting their centers. The magnitude is given by F_g = G * (m1 * m2) / r², where G is the universal gravitational constant (6.67 x 10⁻¹¹ Nm²/kg²), m1 and m2 are the masses of the two objects, and r is the distance between their centers. This law explains why planets orbit the Sun. The gravitational force of the Sun provides the necessary centripetal force (F_c = mv²/r) to keep a planet in a curved path. For a planet of mass m_p in a circular orbit of radius r around the Sun of mass M_s, the centripetal force is provided by gravity: m_p v² / r = G M_s m_p / r². This simplifies to v² = G M_s / r. Since the orbital speed v = 2πr/T, substituting and rearranging gives T²/r³ = 4π²/(GM_s), which is Kepler's Third Law. The value of the constant K is 4π²/(GM_s), which is the same for all planets orbiting the Sun. This derivation successfully connects Newton's mechanics with Kepler's empirical laws.
summary: This section introduces Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation, which states that every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers. The gravitational constant G is introduced. The section also explains how this law provides the physical basis for Kepler's laws. It derives that the centripetal force required for a planet's circular orbit is provided by the Sun's gravitational pull. By equating centripetal force (F_c = mv²/r) with the gravitational force, it derives the relationship for orbital speed and shows that it leads to Kepler's Third Law, identifying the constant K as 4π²/(GM_s).
keywords:
• Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation: A law stating that every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
• Universal Gravitational Constant (G): A fundamental physical constant used in the calculation of gravitational forces, with a value of 6.67 x 10⁻¹¹ Nm²/kg².
• Centripetal Force: A force that acts on a body moving in a circular path and is directed toward the center around which the body is moving.
• Orbital Speed: The speed at which an object travels in its orbit around another object.

notes: Fluid statics is the study of fluids at rest. Matter exists in three states: solid (fixed shape and volume, atoms vibrate at fixed positions), liquid (fixed volume but takes the shape of its container, atoms can slide past each other), and gas (no fixed shape or volume, atoms are far apart and move freely). Fluids (liquids and gases) cannot resist shear (tangential) stress; they flow under any such force. The normal stress in a fluid at rest is called pressure. Pressure is defined as the normal force per unit area, P = F/A. The SI unit of pressure is the Pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m². Other units include atmosphere (atm), mmHg, torr, and psi. Absolute pressure is the total pressure measured relative to a perfect vacuum. Gauge pressure is the pressure measured relative to the local atmospheric pressure: P_gauge = P_abs - P_atm. Density (ρ) is the mass per unit volume of a substance, ρ = m/V. Specific gravity (or relative density) is the ratio of a substance's density to the density of a reference substance, usually water at 4°C. The ideal gas law, PV = nRT = (m/M)RT = ρR_specific T, relates the pressure, volume, temperature, and mass of a gas, providing a link between density and pressure for gases.
summary: This section introduces the fundamental concepts of fluid mechanics, focusing on fluids at rest (fluid statics). It explains the differences between solids, liquids, and gases in terms of molecular arrangement, intermolecular forces, and compressibility. Pressure is defined as force per unit area (P = F/A), and its SI unit (the Pascal) and other common units are introduced. The concepts of absolute pressure, gauge pressure, and atmospheric pressure are defined, along with their relationship (P_abs = P_gauge + P_atm). The section also covers density (ρ = m/V) and its measurement, specific gravity (relative density), and the ideal gas law (PV = nRT) as it relates to the density and pressure of gases.
keywords:
• Fluid: A substance, such as a liquid or gas, that can flow and does not resist shear stress.
• Fluid Statics: The branch of fluid mechanics that studies fluids at rest.
• Pressure: The normal force exerted by a fluid or solid per unit area.
• Pascal (Pa): The SI unit of pressure, equal to one newton per square meter (N/m²).
• Absolute Pressure: The actual pressure at a given position, measured relative to a perfect vacuum.
• Gauge Pressure: The pressure measured relative to the local atmospheric pressure.
• Atmospheric Pressure: The pressure exerted by the weight of the atmosphere at a given location.
• Density: The mass per unit volume of a substance.
• Specific Gravity (Relative Density): The ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a standard substance, typically water.
• Ideal Gas Law: An equation of state that describes the relationship between the pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of an ideal gas (PV = nRT).

notes: In a fluid at rest, pressure acts equally in all directions at a given point. Pascal's Principle states that a change in pressure applied to an enclosed, static fluid is transmitted undiminished to every point in the fluid and to the walls of the container. This principle is the basis for hydraulic presses and lifts, which amplify force. The output force is F₂ = (A₂/A₁) * F₁. The pressure in a fluid increases with depth due to the weight of the fluid above. For a fluid of density ρ, the pressure at a depth h below the surface is given by P = P₀ + ρgh, where P₀ is the pressure at the surface (often atmospheric pressure). This pressure is independent of the shape or size of the container. Atmospheric pressure is measured using a barometer, which typically uses a column of mercury. The height of the mercury column (h) in a barometer is directly proportional to the atmospheric pressure: P_atm = ρ_mercury * g * h. A manometer is a U-shaped tube used to measure the pressure of a gas. The difference in liquid levels in the two arms (h) indicates the gauge pressure of the gas. For an open manometer, the gas pressure is P_gas = P_atm + ρgh (if P_gas > P_atm) or P_gas = P_atm - ρgh (if P_gas < P_atm).
summary: This section explains how pressure behaves in stationary fluids. It introduces Pascal's Principle, stating that a pressure change applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid. This principle is applied to hydraulic presses, explaining how they can multiply force. The variation of pressure with depth in a fluid is derived as P = P₀ + ρgh, where P₀ is the pressure at the surface. The section also describes the measurement of pressure, including the atmospheric pressure measurement using a barometer and the measurement of gas pressure using a manometer.
keywords:
• Pascal's Principle: A principle stating that a change in pressure applied to an enclosed static fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and the container walls.
• Hydraulic Press: A machine that uses Pascal's Principle to multiply force, using two pistons of different areas connected by a fluid.
• Barometer: A device used to measure atmospheric pressure.
• Manometer: A U-shaped device used to measure the pressure of a gas, often relative to atmospheric pressure.
• Hydrostatic Pressure: The pressure exerted by a fluid at rest due to the weight of the fluid above it (P = ρgh).

notes: A fluid exerts an upward force on any object submerged in it, known as the buoyant force (or upthrust). This force arises because the pressure in a fluid increases with depth, resulting in a greater upward force on the bottom of the object than the downward force on the top. Archimedes' Principle states that the magnitude of the buoyant force on an object is equal to the weight of the fluid that the object displaces. Mathematically, F_B = ρ_fluid * g * V_disp, where V_disp is the volume of fluid displaced. For a totally submerged object, V_disp = V_obj. The net force on the object is F_net = F_B - W = (ρ_fluid - ρ_obj) * g * V_obj. Therefore, if ρ_obj < ρ_fluid, the object accelerates upward (floats). If ρ_obj > ρ_fluid, the object sinks. If ρ_obj = ρ_fluid, the object remains in equilibrium at any depth. For an object that floats (partially submerged), the buoyant force equals the object's weight: ρ_fluid * g * V_disp = ρ_obj * g * V_obj. This simplifies to V_disp/V_obj = ρ_obj/ρ_fluid, meaning the fraction of the floating object that is submerged is equal to the ratio of its density to the fluid's density.
summary: This section focuses on the buoyant force, which is the upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object. Archimedes' Principle is stated: the buoyant force on an object is equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces (F_B = ρ_fluid * g * V_disp). The section explains the origin of this force (pressure increasing with depth). It analyzes the conditions for a submerged object to sink, float, or remain suspended based on the comparison of its density to that of the fluid. For a floating object, the fraction of its volume submerged is equal to the ratio of its density to the fluid's density (V_disp/V_obj = ρ_obj/ρ_fluid).
keywords:
• Buoyant Force: The upward force exerted by a fluid on any object immersed in it.
• Archimedes' Principle: A principle stating that the buoyant force on an object is equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
• Upthrust: Another term for the buoyant force.
• Apparent Weight: The weight of an object when submerged in a fluid, which is less than its true weight due to the buoyant force.

notes: Fluid flow is classified into two main types: steady (or laminar) flow and turbulent flow. In steady or laminar flow, every fluid particle follows a smooth path (streamline), and the paths of different particles never cross. The velocity at any given point is constant in time. Turbulent flow is irregular and chaotic, characterized by eddies and mixing of fluid layers. A streamline is the path followed by a fluid particle in steady flow. The flow rate (Q) is the volume of fluid passing through a given area per unit time, Q = V/t. Its SI unit is m³/s. For an incompressible fluid, the principle of conservation of mass requires that the flow rate be constant throughout a pipe or flow tube. This leads to the equation of continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, where A and v are the cross-sectional area and fluid speed at two different points in the pipe. This equation shows that where the pipe is narrower (smaller A), the fluid speed must be higher, and vice versa.
summary: This section covers the behavior of fluids in motion. It distinguishes between steady (laminar) flow, where fluid particles follow smooth, non-crossing paths, and turbulent flow, which is irregular and chaotic. The concept of flow rate (Q = V/t) is introduced. The equation of continuity (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂) is derived and stated, which expresses the principle of mass conservation for an incompressible fluid, showing that the product of cross-sectional area and fluid speed remains constant along a flow tube.
keywords:
• Steady (Laminar) Flow: Fluid flow in which each particle follows a smooth, non-crossing path, and the velocity at any point is constant in time.
• Turbulent Flow: Irregular, chaotic fluid flow characterized by eddies and mixing.
• Flow Rate: The volume of fluid that passes through a given area per unit time (Q = V/t).
• Equation of Continuity: A principle for fluid flow stating that for an incompressible fluid, the product of cross-sectional area and fluid speed is constant along a flow tube (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂).
• Streamline: The path followed by a fluid particle in steady flow.
• Viscosity: A measure of a fluid's resistance to flow, representing internal friction between adjacent layers of fluid.
• Bernoulli's Principle: A principle stating that an increase in the speed of a fluid occurs simultaneously with a decrease in pressure or a decrease in the fluid's potential energy.

Safety and High Pressure concerns the practical challenges and risks associated with systems involving large fluid pressures (gases and liquids). * Structural Integrity: High pressure exerts enormous forces on container walls and joints (F=P×A). Design must account for material strength and stress to prevent rupture (e.g., pressure cookers, deep-sea submersibles, pipelines). * Hydraulic Systems: While high pressure enables force multiplication (Pascal's principle), it requires precise component machining and durable seals to prevent dangerous leaks or failure. * Gas Cylinders: Compressed gases (high pressure) are routinely used but pose explosion hazards if damaged or heated, emphasizing the need for robust cylinders and pressure relief valves. * Deep Sea Diving: Divers must manage the immense hydrostatic pressure at depth to prevent decompression sickness (the bends), which is a physiological response to pressure changes and gas solubility (Henry's Law). * Pressure Measurement: Accurate and calibrated gauges are essential for safe system operation, ensuring pressure limits are never exceeded.
